    @Upsert(conflictsOn = "email")
    Passenger upsertByEmail(Passenger passenger)

    @Upsert(conflictsOn = "email")
    List<Passenger> upsertByEmail(Iterable<Passenger> passengers)

    @Upsert(conflictsOn = "email")
    CompletableFuture<Passenger> upsertByEmailFuture(Passenger passenger)

    @Upsert(conflictsOn = "email")
    CompletableFuture<List<Passenger>> upsertByEmailFuture(Iterable<Passenger> passengers)
}

The same repository method shapes are supported for reactive repositories where the repository type supports those return types. The following R2DBC example returns a Mono for one flight and a Flux for an iterable of flights:

@R2dbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.POSTGRES)
public interface FlightRepository extends CrudRepository<Flight, String> {

    @Upsert
    Mono<Flight> upsertMono(Flight flight);

    @Upsert
    Flux<Flight> upsertFlux(Iterable<Flight> flights);
}
@R2dbcRepository(dialect=Dialect.POSTGRES)
class FlightRepository(CrudRepository[Flight, str]):

    @Upsert
    def upsertMono(self, flight: Flight) -> Mono[Flight]: ...

    @Upsert
    def upsertFlux(self, flights: list[Flight]) -> Flux[Flight]: ...
@R2dbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.POSTGRES)
interface FlightRepository : KotlinCrudRepository<Flight, String> {

    @Upsert
    fun upsertMono(flight: Flight): Mono<Flight>

    @Upsert
    fun upsertFlux(flights: Iterable<Flight>): Flux<Flight>
}
@R2dbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.POSTGRES)
interface FlightRepository extends CrudRepository<Flight, String> {

    @Upsert
    Mono<Flight> upsertMono(Flight flight)

    @Upsert
    Flux<Flight> upsertFlux(Iterable<Flight> flights)
}

Conflict Targets

When conflictsOn is not specified, Micronaut Data uses the entity identity properties to decide whether the upsert should update an existing row.

When conflictsOn is specified, those properties define the conflict target. For example, the PassengerRepository methods above use the unique email property.

Conflict properties must resolve to persistent, non-generated properties. Micronaut Data does not infer the conflict target from every unique constraint on the table. The database schema should still define a primary key or unique constraint that matches the conflict target used by the repository method. That database constraint is what makes the operation reliable under concurrent writes.

Updatable, non-conflict persistent properties are updated when a matching row is found. Identifier properties and conflict properties are preserved as needed by the generated statement. All bindable columns required by the generated statement are available to the insert branch. Properties annotated with @AutoPopulated(updatable = false), including @DateCreated, remain available to the insert branch but are omitted from the matched update branch.

Supported SQL Dialects

Micronaut Data generates dialect-specific SQL for upsert operations.

Dialect Generated SQL shape Notes

Dialect.H2

MERGE INTO <table> target USING (VALUES (…​)) source (…​) ON (…​) WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE …​ WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT …​

The explicit matched and unmatched branches allow insert-only properties to be omitted from updates. The match condition uses the identity columns or configured conflict properties.

Dialect.MYSQL

INSERT INTO <table> (…​) VALUES (…​) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE …​

Used for MySQL-compatible databases, including MariaDB. Unlike dialects with an explicit conflict target, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE reacts to a conflict on any primary-key or unique constraint. The schema should avoid unrelated unique constraints that could select a row other than the one identified by conflictsOn.

Dialect.POSTGRES

INSERT INTO <table> (…​) VALUES (…​) ON CONFLICT (…​) DO UPDATE SET …​

The ON CONFLICT columns are the identity columns or the configured conflict properties. If there are no mutable columns to update, Micronaut Data generates DO NOTHING.

Dialect.SQLITE

INSERT INTO <table> (…​) VALUES (…​) ON CONFLICT (…​) DO UPDATE SET …​

The ON CONFLICT columns are the identity columns or the configured conflict properties. If there are no mutable columns to update, Micronaut Data generates DO NOTHING. SQLite upsert is available through JDBC only.

Dialect.SQL_SERVER

MERGE INTO <table> WITH (HOLDLOCK) AS target USING (VALUES (…​)) AS source (…​) ON …​

The generated MERGE uses WITH (HOLDLOCK) to make the match and write atomic for the target key. Generated identity returning uses OUTPUT inserted.<id-column> when supported.

Dialect.ORACLE

MERGE INTO <table> target USING (SELECT …​ FROM DUAL) source ON (…​) …​

Oracle uses a single-row SELECT …​ FROM DUAL source. Generated identity returning uses RETURNING <id-column> INTO ? when supported.

Dialect.ANSI

MERGE INTO <table> target USING (VALUES (…​)) source (…​) ON (…​) …​

This is the generic SQL MERGE form. Actual support depends on the database used with the ANSI dialect.

Execution and Return Values

Single-Entity Upsert

A single-entity upsert method, such as FlightRepository.upsert(Flight), executes the generated upsert statement for one entity.

Generated Identity Values

When the default identity conflict target is used, generated identity properties are rejected because Micronaut Data needs a non-generated value to match an existing row. When conflictsOn is used, the identity can be generated by the database because another property, such as email, is used to find the row.

For a single-entity operation, Micronaut Data applies a generated identity to the entity when the database and driver return it. For an iterable operation, the execution rules described below prevent a generated identity from being assigned to the wrong input entity.

For SQL Server entities using @GeneratedValue(SEQUENCE), the generated identity column must define a default constraint backed by the configured sequence:

DEFAULT NEXT VALUE FOR <sequence>

SQL Server does not allow NEXT VALUE FOR directly in a MERGE statement. Micronaut Data therefore omits the generated identity column from the MERGE insert branch and relies on the column default. Schemas managed with Flyway, Liquibase, or another external tool must define this constraint explicitly. Micronaut Data schema generation creates the sequence before the table and adds the required default constraint. When using a custom sequence definition, also specify ref so Micronaut Data can reference the sequence by name from the column default.

Iterable Upsert and Batch Execution

An iterable upsert method, such as FlightRepository.upsertAll(Iterable<Flight>), applies the same upsert operation to each entity.

upsertAll is a batch operation at the repository API level, but it should not be understood as a portable multi-row SQL statement. Depending on the dialect, driver, and repository implementation, Micronaut Data may use JDBC batching, driver-specific batching, or execute one statement per entity. Each entity still has its own bind values. Returned entities are produced in the same logical order as the input values.

When the identity is assigned by the application, or the entity does not have a generated identity, Micronaut Data uses the available JDBC or R2DBC batch API. The driver still decides whether that batch is sent in one network exchange or as multiple database commands.

When an upsert has a database-generated identity, a generic batch result does not identify which item in a mixed insert/update batch produced each generated value. JDBC and R2DBC therefore execute one statement per entity when returning generated identities, preserving the association between each returned identity and the entity that produced it.

Oracle JDBC also requires per-entity execution because Oracle DML returning cannot be combined with JDBC batch updates.

Transaction Boundaries

If an item in an upsertAll operation fails, previously executed items may remain persisted. The exact behavior depends on the transaction boundary and database driver, regardless of whether Micronaut Data uses batch or per-entity execution. Execute upsertAll within an explicit transaction when all items must commit or roll back together.

Integration with Other Micronaut Data Features

Lifecycle Events and Auto-Populated Properties

A native upsert does not reveal whether it will insert or update a row before the statement executes. Micronaut Data therefore defines upsert lifecycle behavior using the update lifecycle rather than attempting to invoke both persist and update callbacks.

Before the update lifecycle runs, Micronaut Data prepares framework-managed values needed by the insert branch. This populates @DateCreated and other insert-required properties marked with @AutoPopulated(updatable = false). The normal update preparation then populates values such as @DateUpdated. Upsert preparation preserves a non-null @AutoPopulated UUID on the supplied entity. When that UUID is null, Micronaut Data generates a value for the possible insert branch; an updatable UUID is also included in matched update assignments. Declare the property with @AutoPopulated(updatable = false) when the UUID must remain unchanged after insertion, including when callers use fresh entities with null UUID values.

The resulting lifecycle contract is:

  • @PreUpdate and @PostUpdate callbacks run for an upsert, regardless of which database branch is selected.

  • @PrePersist and @PostPersist callbacks do not run.

  • Relation cascades use Cascade.UPDATE; persist-only cascades are not applied.

  • Non-updatable auto-populated properties are bound for inserts but are not included in the matched update assignments.

This behavior ensures that a newly inserted row receives creation and update timestamps while an existing row retains its original creation timestamp.

Because the selected database branch is not known before execution, the supplied entity is prepared for the possible insert branch. When an upsert matches an existing row, a non-updatable auto-populated property on the supplied or returned entity can therefore differ from the value retained in the database. Reload the entity when the persisted value of such a property is required.

Discriminator Multitenancy

For an entity with @TenantId, upsert preparation supplies the current tenant identifier only when the entity does not already have a tenant value. The tenant identifier is not automatically included in the native upsert match condition. That condition uses the entity identity or the properties declared with @Upsert's conflictsOn member.

Consequently, an upsert that supplies a different tenant identifier can match an existing row and update that row’s tenant value. This is consistent with entity update operations, which also do not add a tenant predicate automatically.

To use the tenant identifier as part of conflict resolution, include it in the entity identity or in conflictsOn together with a database constraint that enforces the same uniqueness rule.

Optimistic Locking

Optimistic locking is not supported by the native upsert implementation. Entities with @Version are rejected for upsert methods.

To support optimistic locking in a single native merge statement, the match condition would need to include both the identity and the expected version, for example:

MERGE INTO book b
USING (SELECT ? id, ? version, ? title FROM DUAL) v
ON (b.id = v.id AND b.version = v.version)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET b.title = v.title, b.version = v.version + 1
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (id, version, title)
  VALUES (v.id, v.version, v.title)

However, this makes the WHEN NOT MATCHED branch ambiguous:

  • No row exists for the given id, so insert is valid.

  • A row exists for the id, but its version is different, so the operation should fail with OptimisticLockException.

Because a native upsert cannot portably distinguish those two cases, Micronaut Data does not enforce optimistic locking in the native upsert path. Use an update or save operation when version checking is required.

Pessimistic Locking

Pessimistic locking is available through finder methods such as find*ForUpdate; an upsert does not acquire a preceding row lock itself.

If find*ForUpdate is executed before an upsert operation in the same transaction:

  • If no row exists, there is no row to lock. Another transaction can still insert the same unique key before this transaction writes. This is exactly where database-native upsert is useful: the unique constraint together with MERGE, ON CONFLICT, or the dialect-specific equivalent handles the race atomically.

  • If a row exists, find*ForUpdate locks that row until the transaction completes. A following upsert will update that existing row while the lock is held. However, since the row is already known to exist, a normal update or save is usually clearer than upsert, unless the code intentionally wants the same method to handle both existing and missing rows.

For a simple "insert or update this entity" operation, using find*ForUpdate before upsert is generally unnecessary. It should not fail, but it usually adds an extra query and lock without much benefit. It only makes sense when the application needs to read the existing row under lock, make decisions from its current state, and then write.

JSON Entity Representation

Upsert is not currently supported for entities that use JSON entity representation, including Oracle JSON Duality view entities mapped with @JsonView.

3.4.4 Deleting

Deleting can be performed in a number of ways. To delete everything (use with care!) you can use deleteAll:

@Override
void deleteAll();
def deleteAll(self) -> None: ...
override fun deleteAll()
void deleteAll()
deleteAll does not cascade. Delete all foreign key references first or use delete on all individual items.

To delete by ID or by the value of a property you can specify a parameter that matches a property of an entity:

void delete(String title);
def delete(self, title: str) -> None: ...
fun delete(title: String)
void delete(String title)

Finally, you can also use the deleteBy* pattern (the method must start with delete, remove, erase or eliminate) and any finder expression, for example:

void deleteByTitleLike(String title);
def deleteByTitleLike(self, title: str) -> None: ...
fun deleteByTitleLike(title: String)
void deleteByTitleLike(String title)

You can also specify A custom query for a delete method:

@Query("DELETE FROM Book WHERE title = :title")
void deleteOne(Book book);

@Query("DELETE FROM Book WHERE title = :title")
void deleteMany(Iterable<Book> books);
@Query("DELETE FROM Book WHERE title = :title")
def deleteOne(self, book: Book) -> None: ...

@Query("DELETE FROM Book WHERE title = :title")
def deleteMany(self, books: list[Book]) -> None: ...
@Query("DELETE FROM Book WHERE title = :title")
fun deleteOne(book: Book)

@Query("DELETE FROM Book WHERE title = :title")
fun deleteMany(books: Iterable<Book>)
@Query("DELETE FROM Book WHERE title = :title")
void deleteOne(Book book)

@Query("DELETE FROM Book WHERE title = :title")
void deleteMany(Iterable<Book> books)

3.4.5 Entity Timestamps

It is common to want to add a field that represents the time when an entity was first persisted and the time when it was last updated.

You can annotate a property that is a date type of entity with @DateCreated which will be automatically populated when saving entities and indicates the date a record was created.

You can also annotate a property that is a date type of entity with @DateUpdated which will be automatically populated whenever the entity is updated either via the persist method or when using one of the batch update methods of Micronaut Data.

If you sometimes want to provide values yourself and otherwise let Micronaut Data populate them, you can use the optional skipIfPresent flag:

@DateCreated(skipIfPresent = true)
Instant created;

@DateUpdated(skipIfPresent = true)
Instant updated;
@DateCreated(skipIfPresent = true)
var created: Instant? = null

@DateUpdated(skipIfPresent = true)
var updated: Instant? = null
@DateCreated(skipIfPresent = true)
Instant created

@DateUpdated(skipIfPresent = true)
Instant updated

Behavior:

  • @DateCreated: skipIfPresent = true preserves a non-null value on insert; otherwise Micronaut Data assigns the timestamp.

  • @DateUpdated: skipIfPresent = true preserves a non-null value only for the initial insert. This is useful for imports or backfills where you want to keep an existing "last updated" value when the row is first created.

  • After the row exists, @DateUpdated keeps its normal meaning: on later updates Micronaut Data always refreshes the field to the current timestamp, regardless of skipIfPresent or the current value.

In other words, skipIfPresent on @DateUpdated is an insert-time override, not a way to make the property user-controlled or immutable after the entity has been stored.

If you update the entity with an external SQL statement or custom logic you will need to update the underlying DateUpdated column manually.

JPA Hibernate and Entity Timestamps

The @DateCreated and @DateUpdated annotations require a ValidatorFactory bean to be present in the application context when used with JPA Hibernate. This can be provided by ensuring one of

implementation("io.micronaut:io.micronaut.validation:micronaut-validation")
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micronaut</groupId>
    <artifactId>io.micronaut.validation</artifactId>
    <version>micronaut-validation</version>
</dependency>
[tool.pyronaut.dependencies]
runtime = [
    "io.micronaut:io.micronaut.validation:micronaut-validation",
]

or

implementation("io.micronaut:io.micronaut.beanvalidation:micronaut-hibernate-validator")
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micronaut</groupId>
    <artifactId>io.micronaut.beanvalidation</artifactId>
    <version>micronaut-hibernate-validator</version>
</dependency>
[tool.pyronaut.dependencies]
runtime = [
    "io.micronaut:io.micronaut.beanvalidation:micronaut-hibernate-validator",
]

is added to your project.

3.4.6 Entity Events

Micronaut Data supports defining entity event listeners for JPA, JDBC, R2DBC, MongoDB and Azure Cosmos using either annotations or by implementing the EntityEventListener interface.

The following table lists the available event annotations:

Table 1. Entity Event Listener Annotations

Annotation

Description

@PrePersist

Triggered prior to persisting an object

@PostPersist

Triggered after persisting an object

@PreRemove

Triggered prior to deleting an object (note: doesn’t apply to batch deletes)

@PostRemove

Triggered after to deleting an object (note: doesn’t apply to batch deletes)

@PreUpdate

Triggered prior to updating an object (note: doesn’t apply to batch updates)

@PostUpdate

Triggered after updating an object (note: doesn’t apply to batch updates)
You can also use the equivalent JPA annotations from the jakarta.persistence package, such as jakarta.persistence.PrePersist, if you prefer.

Each event listener annotation can be applied to an instance method of an entity class (a JPA entity or a class annotated with ann:data.annotation.MappedEntity) in which case the method must return void and have zero arguments for example:

package example;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Convert;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.PrePersist;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.MonthDay;
import java.util.Base64;

@Entity
public class Account {
    @GeneratedValue
    @Id
    private Long id;
    private String username;
    private String password;
    @Column(columnDefinition = "date")
    @Convert(converter = MonthDayDateAttributeConverter.class)
    private MonthDay paymentDay;

    public Long getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public void setId(Long id) {
        this.id = id;
    }

    public String getUsername() {
        return username;
    }

    public void setUsername(String username) {
        this.username = username;
    }

    public String getPassword() {
        return password;
    }

    public void setPassword(String password) {
        this.password = password;
    }

    public MonthDay getPaymentDay() {
        return paymentDay;
    }

    public void setPaymentDay(MonthDay paymentDay) {
        this.paymentDay = paymentDay;
    }

    @PrePersist
    void encodePassword() {
        this.password = Base64.getEncoder()
                .encodeToString(this.password.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    }
}
import base64
from dataclasses import dataclass
from java.time import MonthDay
from typing import Annotated

from jakarta.persistence import Column, Convert, Entity, GeneratedValue, Id, PrePersist

from example.MonthDayDateAttributeConverter import MonthDayDateAttributeConverter


@Entity
@dataclass
class Account:
    username: str | None = None
    password: str | None = None
    paymentDay: Annotated[MonthDay | None, Column(columnDefinition="date"), Convert(converter=MonthDayDateAttributeConverter)] = None
    id: Annotated[int | None, Id, GeneratedValue] = None

    @PrePersist
    def encode_password(self) -> None:
        self.password = base64.b64encode(self.password.encode("utf-8")).decode("ascii")
package example

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets
import java.util.*
import jakarta.persistence.*

@Entity
data class Account(@GeneratedValue @Id
                   var id: Long? = null,
                   val username: String,
                   var password: String) {

    @PrePersist
    fun encodePassword() {
        password = Base64.getEncoder()
            .encodeToString(password.toByteArray(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
    }
}
package example

import jakarta.persistence.*
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets

@Entity
class Account {
    @GeneratedValue
    @Id
    Long id
    String username
    String password

    @PrePersist
    void encodePassword() {
        this.password = Base64.encoder
                .encodeToString(this.password.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
    }
}

The above example defines a @PrePersist listener that encodes the password (in a not very secure base64 format, clearly not recommended!) prior to inserting into the database.

In addition, the annotations can be applied to any instance method of a Micronaut bean, in which case the method must return void and have a single argument that is the entity type (note the type can be Object to listener for all events). For example:

package example;

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.event.PrePersist;

import jakarta.inject.Singleton;

@Singleton
public class AccountUsernameValidator {
    @PrePersist
    void validateUsername(Account account) {
        final String username = account.getUsername();
        if (username == null || !username.matches("[a-z0-9]+")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid username");
        }
    }
}
import re

from jakarta.inject import Singleton
from jakarta.persistence import PrePersist

from example.Account import Account


@Singleton
class AccountUsernameValidator:

    @PrePersist
    def validate_username(self, account: Account) -> None:
        username = account.username
        if username is None or not re.fullmatch("[a-z0-9]+", username):
            raise ValueError("Invalid username")
package example

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.event.PrePersist
import jakarta.inject.Singleton

@Singleton
class AccountUsernameValidator {
    @PrePersist
    fun validateUsername(account: Account) {
        val username: String = account.username
        require(username.matches("[a-z0-9]+".toRegex())) { "Invalid username" }
    }
}
package example

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.event.PrePersist

import jakarta.inject.Singleton

@Singleton
class AccountUsernameValidator {
    @PrePersist
    void validateUsername(Account account) {
        final String username = account.username
        if (!username || !(username ==~ /[a-z0-9]+/)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid username")
        }
    }
}

The above listener serves to validate the account username prior to any insert.

Finally, it is also possible to define a Micronaut bean that implements the EntityEventListener interface or one of the functional interfaces that are sub-interfaces of the EntityEventListener listed in the following table:

Table 2. Entity Event Listener Interfaces

Interface

Description

PrePersistEventListener

Triggered prior to persisting an object

@PostPersistEventListener

Triggered after persisting an object

@PreRemoveEventListener

Triggered prior to deleting an object (note: doesn’t apply to batch deletes)

@PostRemoveEventListener

Triggered after to deleting an object (note: doesn’t apply to batch deletes)

@PreUpdateEventListener

Triggered prior to updating an object (note: doesn’t apply to batch updates)

@PostUpdateEventListener

Triggered after updating an object (note: doesn’t apply to batch updates)

For example the following Micronaut factory bean defines listeners that are executed before and after the Book entity is persisted:

package example;

import io.micronaut.context.annotation.Factory;
import io.micronaut.data.event.listeners.PostPersistEventListener;
import io.micronaut.data.event.listeners.PrePersistEventListener;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

import jakarta.inject.Singleton;

@Factory
public class BookListeners {
    private static final Logger LOG = LoggerFactory.getLogger(BookListeners.class);

    @Singleton
    PrePersistEventListener<Book> beforeBookPersist() { // (1)
        return (book) -> {
            LOG.debug("Inserting book: {}", book.getTitle() );
            return true; // (2)
        };
    }

    @Singleton
    PostPersistEventListener<Book> afterBookPersist() { // (3)
        return (book) -> LOG.debug("Book inserted: {}", book.getTitle() );
    }
}
import logging

from jakarta.inject import Singleton
from micronaut.context.annotation import Factory
from micronaut.data.event.listeners import PostPersistEventListener, PrePersistEventListener

from example.Book import Book

LOG = logging.getLogger(__name__)


@Factory
class BookListeners:

    @Singleton
    def before_book_persist(self) -> PrePersistEventListener[Book]:  # (1)
        def listener(book):
            LOG.debug("Inserting book: %s", book.title)
            return True  # (2)
        return listener

    @Singleton
    def after_book_persist(self) -> PostPersistEventListener[Book]:  # (3)
        return lambda book: LOG.debug("Book inserted: %s", book.title)
package example

import io.micronaut.context.annotation.Factory
import io.micronaut.data.event.listeners.PostPersistEventListener
import io.micronaut.data.event.listeners.PrePersistEventListener
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory
import jakarta.inject.Singleton

@Factory
class BookListeners {
    @Singleton
    fun beforeBookPersist(): PrePersistEventListener<Book> { // (1)
        return PrePersistEventListener { book: Book ->
            LOG.debug("Inserting book: ${book.title}")
            true // (2)
        }
    }

    @Singleton
    fun afterBookPersist(): PostPersistEventListener<Book> { // (3)
        return PostPersistEventListener { book: Book ->
            LOG.debug("Book inserted: ${book.title}")
        }
    }

    companion object {
        private val LOG = LoggerFactory.getLogger(BookListeners::class.java)
    }
}
package example

import io.micronaut.context.annotation.Factory
import io.micronaut.data.event.listeners.PostPersistEventListener
import io.micronaut.data.event.listeners.PrePersistEventListener
import org.slf4j.Logger
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory

import jakarta.inject.Singleton

@Factory
class BookListeners {
    private static final Logger LOG = LoggerFactory.getLogger(BookListeners)

    @Singleton
    PrePersistEventListener<Book> beforeBookPersist() { // (1)
        return (book) -> {
            LOG.debug "Inserting book: ${book.title}"
            return true // (2)
        }
    }

    @Singleton
    PostPersistEventListener<Book> afterBookPersist() { // (3)
        return (book) -> LOG.debug("Book inserted: ${book.title}")
    }
}
1 The factory returns a bean of type PrePersistEventListener that includes Book as the generic argument
2 The PrePersistListener can return false if the operation should not proceed, if this case true is returned
3 An additional @PostPersistEventListener event listener is defined

3.4.7 Exception Handling

Repository methods do not declare checked exceptions. Errors are reported with unchecked exceptions, most of them subclasses of DataAccessException in the io.micronaut.data.exceptions package.

Table 1. Micronaut Data exceptions

Exception

Thrown when

DataAccessException

The base class of the exceptions below. Also thrown directly for datastore errors that have no more specific type. With JDBC, every SQLException is wrapped in a DataAccessException (or one of its subclasses), and the original SQLException is available with getCause().

EntityExistsException

An insert violated a primary key or unique constraint, for example insert was called for an entity whose ID already exists (JDBC and R2DBC).

DataIntegrityViolationException

A write violated another integrity constraint, for example a NOT NULL column received null, or a foreign key refers to a row that does not exist (JDBC and R2DBC).

OptimisticLockException

An update or delete of an entity with a @Version property matched no row, because the row was modified or deleted since the entity was read. See Optimistic locking.

EmptyResultException

A query method whose return type is neither Optional nor nullable found no result.

NonUniqueResultException

A query that must return a single result found more than one.

Behaviour of the CRUD operations

The following applies to the methods inherited from CrudRepository and to the equivalent query methods:

  • Inserting (insert, insertAll, or save of a new entity): a duplicate ID or unique value fails with EntityExistsException, any other constraint violation with DataIntegrityViolationException.

  • Updating and deleting (update, updateAll, delete, deleteAll, and save of an existing entity): for an entity with a @Version property, the statement only matches the row with the same ID and version, and fails with OptimisticLockException when there is none. For an entity without a version property, updating or deleting an entity that does not exist is not an error: nothing is changed. The same applies to deleteById with an unknown ID. With MongoDB, save of an unversioned entity that resolves to an update fails with OptimisticLockException if no document matches.

  • Finding: findById returns an empty Optional if the entity does not exist. A query method that declares a non-nullable single result, for example Book getByTitle(String title), throws EmptyResultException instead; declare the return type as Optional<Book> or annotate it with @Nullable to get an empty result instead. If a single-result query matches more than one row, SQL repositories return the first row by default. Set datasources.<name>.unique-result-on-find-one to true (JDBC) to fail with NonUniqueResultException instead.

  • Null arguments: arguments are not nullable unless annotated with @Nullable. A null ID, entity or collection of entities is rejected with IllegalArgumentException before any statement is executed. Asynchronous and reactive repositories report it through their return type, as described below.

  • Validation: if Micronaut Validation is on the classpath and the type arguments of the repository carry constraints, for example CrudRepository<@Valid Book, @NotNull Long>, invalid arguments are rejected with jakarta.validation.ConstraintViolationException before any statement is executed. See Validation.

Differences between datastores

  • JDBC: all errors are DataAccessException or one of its subclasses, and they are thrown by the repository call that executed the statement.

  • R2DBC: duplicate keys and constraint violations are mapped to EntityExistsException and DataIntegrityViolationException; other R2dbcException errors are propagated unchanged.

  • MongoDB: the Micronaut Data exceptions for missing, non-unique and stale (versioned) results apply, but errors reported by the MongoDB driver, for example com.mongodb.MongoWriteException for a duplicate key, are propagated unchanged.

  • Hibernate JPA and Hibernate Reactive: the query related exceptions (EmptyResultException) are raised by Micronaut Data, but write errors are the exceptions of the JPA provider, for example jakarta.persistence.OptimisticLockException, jakarta.persistence.EntityExistsException or org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException, all subclasses of jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException. Because Hibernate writes changes when the persistence context is flushed, a constraint violation is often only reported when the transaction commits, and is then thrown by the method that ends the transaction rather than by the repository call.

  • Repositories that implement Jakarta Data interfaces convert these exceptions to the jakarta.data.exceptions types required by that specification. See Jakarta Data.

Asynchronous and reactive repositories

Asynchronous and reactive repositories report the same exceptions, but through their return type rather than by throwing:

  • A CompletableFuture / CompletionStage completes exceptionally. CompletableFuture.get() wraps the exception in an ExecutionException and join() in a CompletionException; call getCause() to obtain the Micronaut Data exception. Note that findById of AsyncCrudRepository completes with EmptyResultException when the entity does not exist.

  • A Publisher, Mono or Flux signals the exception with onError. A lookup that finds nothing completes without emitting an item.

  • A Kotlin suspend function throws the exception from the suspending call.

Exceptions and transactions

If an exception escapes a method annotated with @Transactional, the transaction is rolled back by default, whether the exception is checked or unchecked. Use the rollbackOn and dontRollbackOn members of the annotation to change this. Catching a Micronaut Data exception inside the transaction does not undo a rollback-only mark: if a nested transactional call that joined the transaction failed, the transaction is marked as rollback-only and the commit at the end of the outer transaction fails with io.micronaut.transaction.exceptions.UnexpectedRollbackException. In addition, many databases do not allow further statements in a transaction after a failed statement. To recover from an expected error such as a duplicate key, execute the risky operation in its own transaction (REQUIRES_NEW) or nested transaction (NESTED).

3.5 Jakarta Data

Micronaut Data provides implementation support for the Jakarta Data specification, allowing developers to leverage Jakarta Data’s standardized approach to data access within Micronaut applications. This integration combines Micronaut’s efficient Ahead of Time (AoT) compilation capabilities with Jakarta Data’s standardized repository pattern. The Jakarta Data specification provides an API to simplify data access. It enables the Java developer to focus on the data model, while delegating away the complexities of data persistence. To make this possible, Jakarta Data includes a variety of features such as pre-built interfaces for data access, offset and cursor based pagination strategies, and the ability to compose custom query methods that the framework implements.

Configuration

To use Jakarta Data annotations in your Micronaut project, ensure you have the following dependency:

implementation("jakarta.data:jakarta.data-api")
<dependency>
    <groupId>jakarta.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>jakarta.data-api</artifactId>
</dependency>
[tool.pyronaut.dependencies]
runtime = [
    "jakarta.data:jakarta.data-api",
]

Key features

Micronaut Data supports a combination of Jakarta Data annotations and repositories with Micronaut annotations. It’s still required to use @JdbcRepository, @MongoRepository etc to specify which data implementation should be used.

Core Repository Features

  • Repository pattern with annotation @Repository

  • Standard CRUD operations out of the box

  • Type-safe query methods

  • Automatic query derivation from method names

Query Capabilities

  • Method name-based query generation

  • Custom queries with annotation @Query

  • Dynamic finder methods with @Find

  • Result ordering with @OrderBy

  • Limiting results with Limit, and offset or cursor based pagination with PageRequest

Data Modification

  • Entity insertion with @Insert

  • Updates with @Update

  • Persistence with @Save

  • Deletion with @Delete

Repository Mapping

The implementation combines the benefits of Micronaut’s efficient compilation and runtime characteristics with Jakarta Data’s standardized approach to data access.

For more detailed information about individual features and capabilities, please refer to the official Micronaut Data documentation and the Jakarta Data specification.

Jakarta Data Annotations

@Repository

The core annotation that marks an interface as a Jakarta Data repository.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    // repository methods
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    // repository methods
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    // repository methods
}
The default implementation is for JPA, add @JdbcRepository, @MongoRepository etc. for correct implementation

@OrderBy

Specifies the ordering of query results. The annotation is repeatable; each occurrence adds one sort criterion, applied in the order declared.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    @Find
    @OrderBy("lastName")
    @OrderBy("firstName")
    List<User> findAll();
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Find
    @OrderBy("lastName")
    @OrderBy("firstName")
    fun findAll(): List<User>
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Find
    @OrderBy("lastName")
    @OrderBy("firstName")
    List<User> findAll()
}

Query Annotations

@Find

Defines a query from the method parameters: each parameter annotated with @By restricts the entity attribute it names. The method name is not parsed.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    @Find
    List<User> byEmail(@By("email") String email);
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Find
    fun byEmail(@By("email") email: String): List<User>
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Find
    List<User> byEmail(@By("email") String email)
}

@Query

Specifies a custom query string.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.status = :status")
    List<User> findByCustomQuery(String status);
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.status = :status")
    fun findByCustomQuery(status: String): List<User>
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.status = :status")
    List<User> findByCustomQuery(String status)
}

@Save

Conditionally performs insert or update operations on entities. Acts as insert for new entities and update for existing ones.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    @Save
    User save(User user);
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Save
    fun save(user: User): User
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Save
    User save(User user)
}

@Update

Updates the state of existing entities in the database. Throws an exception if entity doesn’t exist.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    @Update
    User update(User user);
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Update
    fun update(user: User): User
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Update
    User update(User user)
}

@Insert

Adds new entities to the database. Throws an exception if entity with same ID already exists.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    @Insert
    User insert(User user);
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Insert
    fun insert(user: User): User
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Insert
    User insert(User user)
}

@Delete

Removes entities from the database.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    @Delete
    void delete(User user);
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Delete
    fun delete(user: User)
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Delete
    void delete(User user)
}

Method Parameters

@Param

Names a method parameter for use in queries.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.department = :dept")
    List<User> findByDepartment(@Param("dept") String department);
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.department = :dept")
    fun findByDepartment(@Param("dept") department: String): List<User>
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.department = :dept")
    List<User> findByDepartment(@Param("dept") String department)
}

Limiting results

Pass a jakarta.data.Limit parameter to restrict the number of results. Limit.of(10) returns at most 10 results, and Limit.range(21, 30) returns results 21 to 30 (positions start at 1), which also covers offset based access. For paging with totals use PageRequest as described in Pagination below.

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName, Limit limit);
}

// usage
userRepository.findByLastName("Smith", Limit.of(10));
userRepository.findByLastName("Smith", Limit.range(21, 30));
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    fun findByLastName(lastName: String, limit: Limit): List<User>
}

// usage
userRepository.findByLastName("Smith", Limit.of(10))
userRepository.findByLastName("Smith", Limit.range(21, 30))
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName, Limit limit)
}

// usage
userRepository.findByLastName("Smith", Limit.of(10))
userRepository.findByLastName("Smith", Limit.range(21, 30))

Repository Method Conventions

Besides annotations, Jakarta Data also supports method name conventions for common queries:

@Repository
public interface UserRepository {
    // Derived finder methods
    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName);
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);
    List<User> findByAgeGreaterThan(int age);

    // Count methods
    long countByStatus(String status);

    // Existence checks
    boolean existsByEmail(String email);

    // Delete methods
    void deleteByLastName(String lastName);
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    // Derived finder methods
    fun findByLastName(lastName: String): List<User>
    fun findByEmail(email: String): Optional<User>
    fun findByAgeGreaterThan(age: Int): List<User>

    // Count methods
    fun countByStatus(status: String): Long

    // Existence checks
    fun existsByEmail(email: String): Boolean

    // Delete methods
    fun deleteByLastName(lastName: String)
}
@Repository
interface UserRepository {
    // Derived finder methods
    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName)
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email)
    List<User> findByAgeGreaterThan(int age)

    // Count methods
    long countByStatus(String status)

    // Existence checks
    boolean existsByEmail(String email)

    // Delete methods
    void deleteByLastName(String lastName)
}

Pagination

Offset Pagination

Example of different pagination approaches:

Page<Book> slice = bookRepository.list(PageRequest.ofSize(3));
List<Book> resultList =
		bookRepository.findByPagesGreaterThan(500, PageRequest.ofSize(3));
Page<Book> page = bookRepository.findByTitleLike("The%", PageRequest.ofSize(3));
val slice: Page<Book> = bookRepository.list(PageRequest.ofSize(3))
val resultList: List<Book> =
    bookRepository.findByPagesGreaterThan(500, PageRequest.ofSize(3))
val page: Page<Book> = bookRepository.findByTitleLike("The%", PageRequest.ofSize(3))
Page<Book> slice = bookRepository.list(PageRequest.ofSize(3))
List<Book> resultList =
        bookRepository.findByPagesGreaterThan(500, PageRequest.ofSize(3))
Page<Book> page = bookRepository.findByTitleLike("The%", PageRequest.ofSize(3))

Cursor-based Pagination

Advanced pagination with cursors and sorting:

Sort<Object> order = Sort.asc("title");
CursoredPage<Book> page =  // (1)
    bookRepository.find(PageRequest.ofSize(5), order);
CursoredPage<Book> page2 = bookRepository.find(page.nextPageRequest(), order); // (2)
CursoredPage<Book> pageByPagesBetween = // (3)
    bookRepository.findByPagesBetween(400, 700, PageRequest.ofSize(3));
Page<Book> pageByTitleStarts = // (4)
    bookRepository.findByTitleStartingWith("The", PageRequest.ofSize( 3));
val order: Sort<Any> = Sort.asc("title")
val page: CursoredPage<Book> = // (1)
    bookRepository.find(PageRequest.ofSize(5), order)
val page2: CursoredPage<Book> = bookRepository.find(page.nextPageRequest(), order) // (2)
val pageByPagesBetween: CursoredPage<Book> = // (3)
    bookRepository.findByPagesBetween(400, 700, PageRequest.ofSize(3))
val pageByTitleStarts: Page<Book> = // (4)
    bookRepository.findByTitleStartingWith("The", PageRequest.ofSize(3))
Sort<Object> order = Sort.asc("title")
CursoredPage<Book> page = // (1)
        bookRepository.find(PageRequest.ofSize(5), order)
CursoredPage<Book> page2 = bookRepository.find(page.nextPageRequest(), order) // (2)
CursoredPage<Book> pageByPagesBetween = // (3)
        bookRepository.findByPagesBetween(400, 700, PageRequest.ofSize(3))
Page<Book> pageByTitleStarts = // (4)
        bookRepository.findByTitleStartingWith("The", PageRequest.ofSize(3))
1 Create a page with sorting by title
2 Get the next page using cursor
3 Find books with pages between specific values
4 Find books with titles starting with a specific string

Jakarta Data Exceptions

Micronaut Data will convert exceptions to Jakarta Data variations only if the repository is annotated with @jakarta.data.repository.Repository or the method is using any other Jakarta Data annotations @jakarta.data.repository.Find, @jakarta.data.repository.Save etc.

3.6 Repositories with Jakarta Criteria API

In some cases, you need to build a query programmatically and at the runtime; for that, Micronaut Data supports Jakarta Persistence Criteria API 3.0.

The API described in this section is the same for every Micronaut Data module. With Micronaut Data JPA the criteria are executed by Hibernate, while Micronaut Data JDBC / R2DBC, MongoDB and Azure Cosmos implement a subset of the Criteria API themselves. For the additional dependency these modules require and the Criteria API features they do not support, see:

  • Criteria API with JDBC / R2DBC

  • Criteria API with MongoDB

  • Criteria API with Azure Cosmos

To implement queries that cannot be defined at the compile-time Micronaut Data introduces JpaSpecificationExecutor repository interface that can be used to extend your repository interface:

JDBC / R2DBC
@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.H2)
@Requires(notEnv="oracle")
public interface PersonRepository extends CrudRepository<Person, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
}
JDBC / R2DBC
@JdbcRepository(dialect=Dialect.H2)
class PersonRepository(CrudRepository[Person, int]):
JDBC / R2DBC
@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.H2)
interface PersonRepository : KotlinCrudRepository<Person, Long>, KotlinJpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
}
JDBC / R2DBC
@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.H2)
interface PersonRepository extends CrudRepository<Person, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
}
MongoDB
@MongoRepository
public interface PersonRepository extends CrudRepository<Person, ObjectId>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
}
MongoDB
@MongoRepository
class PersonRepository(CrudRepository[Person, ObjectId]):
MongoDB
@MongoRepository
interface PersonRepository : CrudRepository<Person, ObjectId>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
    }
MongoDB
@MongoRepository
interface PersonRepository extends CrudRepository<Person, ObjectId>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
}
Azure Cosmos
@CosmosRepository
public interface PersonRepository extends CrudRepository<Person, String>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
}
Azure Cosmos
@CosmosRepository
class PersonRepository(CrudRepository[Person, str]):
Azure Cosmos
@CosmosRepository
interface PersonRepository : CrudRepository<Person, String>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
}
Azure Cosmos
@CosmosRepository
interface PersonRepository extends CrudRepository<Person, String>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Person> {
}

Only the repository annotation and the ID type differ between the modules; with Micronaut Data JPA the repository is annotated with @Repository. The remaining examples in this section use the JDBC example project; the MongoDB and Azure Cosmos example projects declare equivalent methods and specifications, referencing properties by name (for example root.get("name")) instead of through the static metamodel.

In Python declare the specification methods on the repository itself: Micronaut Data matches them by their PredicateSpecification / QuerySpecification / UpdateSpecification / DeleteSpecification parameter types. A specification is a plain Python function or lambda, and since and, or and not are Python keywords, the corresponding CriteriaBuilder methods are called as and_, or_ and not_.

Each method expects a "specification" which is a functional interface with a set of Criteria API objects intended to build a query programmatically.

3.6.1 Querying

To find an entity or multiple entities you can use one of the following methods from JpaSpecificationExecutor interface:

Optional<Person> findOne(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec);

Optional<Person> findOne(QuerySpecification<Person> spec);

List<Person> findAll(@Nullable PredicateSpecification<Person> spec);

List<Person> findAll(QuerySpecification<Person> spec);

List<Person> findAll(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec, Sort sort);

List<Person> findAll(QuerySpecification<Person> spec, Sort sort);

Page<Person> findAll(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec, Pageable pageable);

Page<Person> findAll(QuerySpecification<Person> spec, Pageable pageable);
def findOne(self, spec: PredicateSpecification[Person]) -> Optional[Person]: ...

def findAll(self, spec: PredicateSpecification[Person] | None) -> list[Person]: ...

def findAllSorted(self, spec: PredicateSpecification[Person], sort: Sort) -> list[Person]: ...

def findPage(self, spec: PredicateSpecification[Person], pageable: Pageable) -> Page[Person]: ...
fun findOne(spec: PredicateSpecification<Person>?): Person?

fun findOne(spec: QuerySpecification<Person>?): Person?

fun findAll(spec: PredicateSpecification<Person>?): List<Person>

fun findAll(spec: QuerySpecification<Person>?): List<Person>

fun findAll(spec: PredicateSpecification<Person>?, sort: Sort): List<Person>

fun findAll(spec: QuerySpecification<Person>?, sort: Sort): List<Person>

fun findAll(spec: PredicateSpecification<Person>?, pageable: Pageable): Page<Person>

fun findAll(spec: QuerySpecification<Person>?, pageable: Pageable): Page<Person>
Optional<Person> findOne(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec)

Optional<Person> findOne(QuerySpecification<Person> spec)

List<Person> findAll(@Nullable PredicateSpecification<Person> spec)

List<Person> findAll(QuerySpecification<Person> spec)

List<Person> findAll(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec, Sort sort)

List<Person> findAll(QuerySpecification<Person> spec, Sort sort)

Page<Person> findAll(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec, Pageable pageable)

Page<Person> findAll(QuerySpecification<Person> spec, Pageable pageable)

As you can see, there are two variations of findOne/findAll methods.

First method is expecting PredicateSpecification which is a simple specification interface that can be implemented to return a predicate:

import static jakarta.persistence.criteria.*;

public interface PredicateSpecification<T> {

    (1)
    @Nullable
    Predicate toPredicate(@NonNull Root<T> root, (2)
                          @NonNull CriteriaBuilder criteriaBuilder (3)
    );

}
1 The specification is producing a query limiting predicate
2 The entity root
3 The criteria builder

This interface can also be used for update and delete methods, and it provides or and and methods for combining multiple predicates.

The second interface is intended only for query criteria because it includes jakarta.persistence.criteria.CriteriaQuery as a parameter.

import static jakarta.persistence.criteria.*;

public interface QuerySpecification<T> {

    (1)
    @Nullable
    Predicate toPredicate(@NonNull Root<T> root, (2)
                          @NonNull CriteriaQuery<?> query, (3)
                          @NonNull CriteriaBuilder criteriaBuilder (4)
    );

}
1 The specification is producing a query limiting predicate
2 The entity root
3 The criteria query instance
4 The criteria builder

For implementing counting queries following methods can be used:

long count(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec);

long count(QuerySpecification<Person> spec);
def count(self, spec: PredicateSpecification[Person]) -> int: ...
fun count(spec: PredicateSpecification<Person>?): Long

fun count(spec: QuerySpecification<Person>?): Long
long count(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec)

long count(QuerySpecification<Person> spec)

You can define criteria specification methods that will help you to create a query:

class Specifications {

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> nameEquals(String name) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get(Person_.name), name);
    }

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> longNameEquals(String longName) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get(Person_.longName), longName);
    }

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> ageIsLessThan(int age) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.lessThan(root.get(Person_.age), age);
    }

}
def name_equals(name: str):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.equal(root.get("name"), name)


def long_name_equals(long_name: str):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.equal(root.get("longName"), long_name)


def age_is_less_than(age: int):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.lessThan(root.get("age"), age)


# `and`, `or` and `not` are Python keywords: the trailing underscore maps to the CriteriaBuilder method
def and_(spec, other):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.and_(spec(root, criteria_builder), other(root, criteria_builder))


def or_(spec, other):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.or_(spec(root, criteria_builder), other(root, criteria_builder))


def not_(spec):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.not_(spec(root, criteria_builder))
object Specifications {

    fun nameEquals(name: String?) = PredicateSpecification<Person> { root, criteriaBuilder ->
        criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get<Any>("name"), name)
    }

    fun ageIsLessThan(age: Int) = PredicateSpecification<Person> { root, criteriaBuilder ->
        criteriaBuilder.lessThan(root.get("age"), age)
    }

}
class Specifications {

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> nameEquals(String name) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get("name"), name)
    }

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> ageIsLessThan(int age) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.lessThan(root.get("age"), age)
    }

}

Then you can combine them for find or count queries:

Person denis = personRepository.findOne(nameEquals("Denis")).orElse(null);

Person josh = personRepository.findOne(longNameEquals("Josh PM")).orElse(null);

long countAgeLess30 = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(30));

long countAgeLess20 = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(20));

long countAgeLess30NotDenis = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(30).and(not(nameEquals("Denis"))));

List<Person> people = personRepository.findAll(where(nameEquals("Denis").or(nameEquals("Josh"))));
denis = self.personRepository.findOne(name_equals("Denis")).orElse(None)

josh = self.personRepository.findOne(long_name_equals("Josh PM")).orElse(None)

count_age_less_30 = self.personRepository.count(age_is_less_than(30))

count_age_less_20 = self.personRepository.count(age_is_less_than(20))

count_age_less_30_not_denis = self.personRepository.count(and_(age_is_less_than(30), not_(name_equals("Denis"))))

people = self.personRepository.findAll(or_(name_equals("Denis"), name_equals("Josh")))
val denis: Person? = personRepository.findOne(nameEquals("Denis"))

val countAgeLess30: Long = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(30))

val countAgeLess20: Long = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(20))

val countAgeLess30NotDenis: Long = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(30).and(not(nameEquals("Denis"))))

val people = personRepository.findAll(PredicateSpecification.where(nameEquals("Denis").or(nameEquals("Josh"))))
Person denis = personRepository.findOne(nameEquals("Denis")).orElse(null)

long countAgeLess30 = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(30))

long countAgeLess20 = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(20))

long countAgeLess30NotDenis = personRepository.count(ageIsLessThan(30) & PredicateSpecification.not(nameEquals("Denis")))

List<Person> people = personRepository.findAll(PredicateSpecification.where(nameEquals("Denis") | nameEquals("Josh")))
The examples use compile-known values, and in this case, it would be better to create custom repository methods which would come with compile-time generates queries and eliminate runtime overhead. It’s recommended to use criteria only for dynamic queries where the query structure is not known at the build-time.

With Micronaut Data JDBC / R2DBC, pagination with JOINs cannot be properly implemented by limiting the results for tabular SQL results, because of that Micronaut Data will execute two queries:

  • 1. Fetching a page of entity IDs

  • 2. Fetching a complete entity with JOINed associations

3.6.2 Updating

To implement the update you can use following method from JpaSpecificationExecutor interface:

long updateAll(UpdateSpecification<Person> spec);
def updateAll(self, spec: UpdateSpecification[Person]) -> int: ...
fun updateAll(spec: UpdateSpecification<Person>?): Long
long updateAll(UpdateSpecification<Person> spec)

This method is expecting UpdateSpecification which is a variation of specification interface that includes access to jakarta.persistence.criteria.CriteriaUpdate:

import static jakarta.persistence.criteria.*;

public interface UpdateSpecification<T> {

    (1)
    @Nullable
    Predicate toPredicate(@NonNull Root<T> root, (2)
                          @NonNull CriteriaUpdate<?> query, (3)
                          @NonNull CriteriaBuilder criteriaBuilder (4)
    );

}
1 The specification is producing a query limiting predicate
2 The entity root
3 The criteria update instance
4 The criteria builder

Updating specific properties can be done using jakarta.persistence.criteria.CriteriaUpdate interface:

query.set(root.get(Person_.name), newName);
query.set(root.get("name"), new_name)
query.set(root.get("name"), newName)
query.set(root.get("name"), newName)

You can define criteria specification methods including update specification that will help you to create an update query:

class Specifications {

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> nameEquals(String name) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get(Person_.name), name);
    }

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> longNameEquals(String longName) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get(Person_.longName), longName);
    }

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> ageIsLessThan(int age) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.lessThan(root.get(Person_.age), age);
    }

    static UpdateSpecification<Person> setNewName(String newName) {
        return (root, query, criteriaBuilder) -> {
            query.set(root.get(Person_.name), newName);
            return null;
        };
    }
}
def name_equals(name: str):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.equal(root.get("name"), name)


def long_name_equals(long_name: str):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.equal(root.get("longName"), long_name)


def age_is_less_than(age: int):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.lessThan(root.get("age"), age)


# `and`, `or` and `not` are Python keywords: the trailing underscore maps to the CriteriaBuilder method
def and_(spec, other):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.and_(spec(root, criteria_builder), other(root, criteria_builder))


def or_(spec, other):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.or_(spec(root, criteria_builder), other(root, criteria_builder))


def not_(spec):
    return lambda root, criteria_builder: criteria_builder.not_(spec(root, criteria_builder))


def set_new_name(new_name: str, where):
    def specification(root, query, criteria_builder):
        query.set(root.get("name"), new_name)
        return where(root, criteria_builder)
    return specification
object Specifications {

    fun nameEquals(name: String?) = PredicateSpecification<Person> { root, criteriaBuilder ->
        criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get<Any>("name"), name)
    }

    fun ageIsLessThan(age: Int) = PredicateSpecification<Person> { root, criteriaBuilder ->
        criteriaBuilder.lessThan(root.get("age"), age)
    }

    fun setNewName(newName: String) = UpdateSpecification<Person> { root, query, criteriaBuilder ->
        query.set(root.get("name"), newName)
        null
    }

    fun nameInList(names: List<String>) = where<Person> {
        root[Person::name] inList names
    }

    fun nameOrAgeMatches(name: String, age: Int) = query<Person, Person> {
        where {
            or {
               root[Person::name] eq name
               root[Person::age] eq age
            }
        }
    }

    fun nameMatches(name: String) = query<Person, Person> {
        where {
            or {
               root[Person::name] eq name
            }
        }
    }

    fun updateName(newName: String, existingName: String) = update<Person> {
        set(Person::name, newName)
        where {
            root[Person::name] eq existingName
        }
    }
    fun deleteByName(name: String) = delete<Person> {
        root[Person::name] eq name
    }
}
class Specifications {

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> nameEquals(String name) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get("name"), name)
    }

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> ageIsLessThan(int age) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.lessThan(root.get("age"), age)
    }

    static UpdateSpecification<Person> setNewName(String newName) {
        return (root, query, criteriaBuilder) -> {
            query.set(root.get("name"), newName)
            null
        }
    }
}

Then you can use the update specification combined with predicate specifications:

long recordsUpdated = personRepository.updateAll(setNewName("Steven").where(nameEquals("Denis")));
records_updated = self.personRepository.updateAll(set_new_name("Steven", where=name_equals("Denis")))
val recordsUpdated = personRepository.updateAll(setNewName("Steven").where(nameEquals("Denis")))
long recordsUpdated = personRepository.updateAll(setNewName("Steven").where(nameEquals("Denis")))

3.6.3 Deleting

To delete an entity or multiple entities you can use one of the following methods from JpaSpecificationExecutor interface:

long deleteAll(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec);

long deleteAll(DeleteSpecification<Person> spec);
def deleteAll(self, spec: PredicateSpecification[Person]) -> int: ...
fun deleteAll(spec: PredicateSpecification<Person>?): Long

fun deleteAll(spec: DeleteSpecification<Person>?): Long
long deleteAll(PredicateSpecification<Person> spec)

long deleteAll(DeleteSpecification<Person> spec)

As it is for querying, deleteAll methods also come in two variations.

First method is expecting PredicateSpecification which is the same interface described in Querying section

The second method comes with DeleteSpecification and is intended only for delete criteria because it includes access to jakarta.persistence.criteria.CriteriaDelete.

import static jakarta.persistence.criteria.*;

public interface DeleteSpecification<T> {

    (1)
    @Nullable
    Predicate toPredicate(@NonNull Root<T> root, (2)
                          @NonNull CriteriaDelete<?> query, (3)
                          @NonNull CriteriaBuilder criteriaBuilder (4)
    );

}
1 The specification is producing a query limiting predicate
2 The entity root
3 The criteria delete instance
4 The criteria builder

For deleting you can reuse the same predicates as for querying and updating:

class Specifications {

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> nameEquals(String name) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get(Person_.name), name);

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> longNameEquals(String longName) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.equal(root.get(Person_.longName), longName);
    }

    static PredicateSpecification<Person> ageIsLessThan(int age) {
        return (root, criteriaBuilder) -> criteriaBuilder.lessThan(root.get(Person_.age), age);
    }

}

def or_(spec, other):

long recordsDeleted = personRepository.deleteAll(where(nameEquals("Denis")));
