    @MappedProperty(value = "long_name_column_legacy_system", alias = "long_name")
    private String longName;

    public Person() {
    }

    public Person(String name, int age, String longName) {
        this(null, name, age, longName);
    }

    public Person(Long id, String name, int age, String longName) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
        this.longName = longName;
    }

    public Long getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public void setId(Long id) {
        this.id = id;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    public void setAge(int age) {
        this.age = age;
    }

    public String getLongName() {
        return longName;
    }

    public void setLongName(String longName) {
        this.longName = longName;
    }
}
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Annotated

from micronaut.data.annotation import GeneratedValue, Id, MappedEntity, MappedProperty


@MappedEntity
@dataclass
class Person:
    name: str
    age: int
    longName: Annotated[str | None, MappedProperty(value="long_name_column_legacy_system", alias="long_name")] = None
    id: Annotated[int | None, Id, GeneratedValue] = None
package example

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.Id
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue

@Entity
class Person {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    var id: Long? = null
    var name: String? = null
    var age = 0

    constructor(name: String?, age: Int) : this(null, name, age) {}
    constructor(id: Long?, name: String?, age: Int) {
        this.id = id
        this.name = name
        this.age = age
    }
}
package example

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.Id
import jakarta.persistence.Entity
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue


@Entity
class Person {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id
    private String name
    private int age

    Person() {
    }

    Person(String name, int age) {
        this(null, name, age)
    }

    Person(Long id, String name, int age) {
        this.id = id
        this.name = name
        this.age = age
    }

    Long getId() {
        return id
    }

    void setId(Long id) {
        this.id = id
    }

    String getName() {
        return name
    }

    void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name
    }

    int getAge() {
        return age
    }

    void setAge(int age) {
        this.age = age
    }
}

In this example, original column name long_name_column_legacy_system will be returned in a result from the database as long_name. When alias property is set then be careful when writing custom or native queries to return field as indicated in alias value.

Setting alias in MappedProperty on assocations does not have an effect as it makes sense only on fields/columns mappings.

4.5.11 Geospatial Support

Micronaut Data supports geospatial persistence through Micronaut repositories using the io.micronaut.data.model.geo model types:

  • Point

  • MultiPoint

  • LineString

  • MultiLineString

  • Polygon

  • MultiPolygon

  • GeometryCollection

The implementation is database-aware. Micronaut Data uses JSON and WKT converters in the Java model, and then applies dialect-specific SQL functions when reading from or writing to native spatial columns.

JSON and WKT converters

The model types in io.micronaut.data.model.geo are declared with @TypeDef(type = DataType.STRING, converter = GeometryJsonConverter.class), so GeoJSON is the default mapping.

GeometryJsonConverter converts between Micronaut Data geospatial objects and GeoJSON strings. GeometryWktConverter converts the same model types to and from Well-Known Text (WKT).

Use the default GeoJSON mapping when you want Micronaut Data to serialize geospatial values as JSON:

@MappedEntity
public class GeometryEntityJson {

    @Srid(Srid.WEB_MERCATOR)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty("location")
    private Point point;

    @Nullable
    private MultiPoint multiPoint;
}
@MappedEntity
data class GeometryEntityJson(
    @field:Srid(Srid.WEB_MERCATOR)
    @field:Index(columns = ["location"])
    @MappedProperty("location")
    val point: Point,

    val multiPoint: MultiPoint? = null
)
@MappedEntity
class GeometryEntityJson {

    @Srid(Srid.WEB_MERCATOR)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty("location")
    Point point

    @Nullable
    MultiPoint multiPoint
}

Use @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter.class) when you want WKT conversion instead:

@MappedEntity
public class GeometryEntityWkt {

    @Srid(Srid.WEB_MERCATOR)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter.class)
    private Point point;

    @Nullable
    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter.class)
    private MultiPoint multiPoint;
}
@MappedEntity
data class GeometryEntityWkt(
    @field:Srid(Srid.WEB_MERCATOR)
    @field:Index(columns = ["location"])
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter::class)
    val point: Point,

    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter::class)
    val multiPoint: MultiPoint? = null
)
@MappedEntity
class GeometryEntityWkt {

    @Srid(Srid.WEB_MERCATOR)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter)
    Point point

    @Nullable
    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter)
    MultiPoint multiPoint
}
The converter controls the Java-side representation. The generated SQL still uses database-specific spatial functions and native spatial column definitions when the dialect supports them.

SRID and coordinate reference system type

Use Srid to declare the spatial reference system identifier used for a persistent geospatial property. Micronaut Data uses the SRID value when it generates read and write conversion SQL, schema metadata, and predicate argument conversion.

Use the constants declared on Srid for common spatial reference systems:

  • Srid.WGS_84 (4326) - World Geodetic System 1984

  • Srid.WEB_MERCATOR (3857) - Web Mercator

  • Srid.ETRS_89 (4258) - European Terrestrial Reference System 1989

For example, use @Srid(value = Srid.WGS_84, type = Srid.CrsType.GEOGRAPHIC) for WGS 84 coordinates.

Micronaut Data uses Srid.CrsType to choose the distance function for dialects that have different functions for planar and spherical distance checks:

Dialect Srid.CrsType Distance predicate

MySQL and MariaDB

Srid.CrsType.PROJECTED

ST_Distance(column, convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

MySQL and MariaDB

Srid.CrsType.GEOGRAPHIC

ST_Distance_Sphere(column, convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

H2 / H2GIS

Srid.CrsType.PROJECTED

ST_DWithin(column, convertedValue, distanceValue)

H2 / H2GIS

Srid.CrsType.GEOGRAPHIC

ST_DistanceSphere(column, convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

For the other supported SQL dialects, Srid.CrsType does not currently change the generated Near predicate function. For PostgreSQL / PostGIS and SQL Server, Srid.CrsType.GEOGRAPHIC selects the native GEOGRAPHY column type and matching read and write conversions. Other dialects retain their native geometry column type. An explicit @MappedProperty(definition = "…​") always takes precedence over the inferred column type.

Query predicates

Micronaut Data also translates repository finder methods and criteria predicates for geospatial comparisons into dialect-specific SQL.

For example, the following repository method fragments are supported for SQL dialects with geospatial support:

  • findByLocationGeoWithin(geometry)

  • findByLocationGeoIntersects(geometry)

  • findByLocationNear(geometry, distance)

The same operations are available through the criteria API with geoWithin, geoIntersects, and near predicates.

Micronaut Data applies the same GeoJSON or WKT conversion rules described above to the predicate arguments, and each database section below documents the exact spatial functions emitted for that dialect.

Near expects the second argument to be a numeric distance value. Micronaut Data passes that value through as a bind parameter and uses the most appropriate distance predicate available for the active dialect.

Database vendor details

Each supported SQL dialect uses its own built-in spatial functions for read and write conversion, generates its own spatial column definitions, and emits its own index DDL.

Oracle

Oracle stores spatial values in SDO_GEOMETRY columns.

Micronaut Data uses the following functions to read and write spatial data:

Mapping Read conversion Write conversion Write conversion with SRID

GeoJSON

SDO_UTIL.TO_GEOJSON(column)

SDO_UTIL.FROM_GEOJSON(?)

SDO_UTIL.FROM_GEOJSON(?, NULL, srid)

WKT

SDO_UTIL.TO_WKTGEOMETRY(column)

SDO_UTIL.FROM_WKTGEOMETRY(TO_CHAR(?))

SDO_UTIL.FROM_WKTGEOMETRY(TO_CHAR(?), srid)
Oracle SDO_UTIL.FROM_GEOJSON currently does not accept NULL. The bug has been reported and the fix will be released soon. Until the bug fix gets released, you can use GeoJSON conversion only for geospatial columns that are required. Otherwise you can use WKT conversion.

Schema generation

The Oracle database requires rows in USER_SDO_GEOM_METADATA for spatial columns that are indexed. Micronaut Data generates those metadata statements automatically if you use Micronaut Data’s internal schema-generation tooling, which is intended for tests rather than production schema management. In that case, the generated metadata depends on the SRID. The internal schema-generation tooling currently supports the following SRIDs:

  • Srid.WGS_84 (4326) - WGS 84 - World Geodetic System 1984

  • Srid.WEB_MERCATOR (3857) - Web Mercator

  • Srid.ETRS_89 (4258) - ETRS89 - Geodetic coordinate system for Europe

If using the internal schema-generation tooling and another SRID, a new row will not be inserted into the USER_SDO_GEOM_METADATA table.

In production you will insert those metadata rows using a SQL migration tool such as Flyway or Liquibase.

If using the internal schema-generation tooling, spatial indexes will be created for all columns whose properties are annotated with @Index:

CREATE INDEX "IDX_GEOMETRY_ENTITY_JSON_LOCATION" ON "GEOMETRY_ENTITY_JSON" ("LOCATION") INDEXTYPE IS MDSYS.SPATIAL_INDEX

Query predicates

Micronaut Data translates geospatial repository methods and criteria predicates to the following Oracle spatial functions:

Predicate Oracle spatial function

GeoWithin

SDO_INSIDE(column, convertedValue) = 'TRUE'

GeoIntersects

SDO_ANYINTERACT(column, convertedValue) = 'TRUE'

Near

SDO_WITHIN_DISTANCE(column, convertedValue, 'distance=distanceValue') = 'TRUE'

convertedValue is the Oracle spatial conversion call such as SDO_UTIL.FROM_GEOJSON(?, NULL, srid) or SDO_UTIL.FROM_WKTGEOMETRY(TO_CHAR(?), srid).

PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL geospatial support requires the PostGIS extension because the spatial types, functions, and indexes used by Micronaut Data come from PostGIS.

PostGIS stores spatial values in GEOMETRY or GEOGRAPHY columns. Micronaut Data uses the GEOMETRY column type by default. To change the column type to GEOGRAPHY, set @MappedProperty(definition = "geography"):

@MappedEntity
public class GeographyEntityJson {

    @Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", definition = "geography not null")
    private Point point;

    @Nullable
    @MappedProperty(definition = "geography")
    private MultiPoint multiPoint;
}
@MappedEntity
data class GeographyEntityJson(
    @field:Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @field:Index(columns = ["location"])
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", definition = "geography not null")
    val point: Point,

    @MappedProperty(definition = "geography")
    val multiPoint: MultiPoint? = null
)
@MappedEntity
class GeographyEntityJson {

    @Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", definition = "geography not null")
    Point point

    @Nullable
    @MappedProperty(definition = "geography")
    MultiPoint multiPoint
}

For WKT conversion, use:

@MappedEntity
public class GeographyEntityWkt {

    @Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter.class, definition = "geography not null")
    private Point point;

    @Nullable
    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter.class, definition = "geography")
    private MultiPoint multiPoint;
}
@MappedEntity
data class GeographyEntityWkt(
    @field:Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @field:Index(columns = ["location"])
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter::class, definition = "geography not null")
    val point: Point,

    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter::class, definition = "geography")
    val multiPoint: MultiPoint? = null
)
@MappedEntity
class GeographyEntityWkt {

    @Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter, definition = "geography not null")
    Point point

    @Nullable
    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter, definition = "geography")
    MultiPoint multiPoint
}

Micronaut Data uses the following functions to read and write spatial data:

Mapping Read conversion Write conversion Write conversion with SRID

GeoJSON

ST_AsGeoJSON(column)

ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?)

ST_SetSRID(ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?), srid)

WKT

ST_AsText(column)

ST_GeomFromText(?)

ST_GeomFromText(?, srid)

For GEOGRAPHY data type Micronaut Data still uses the same ST_GeomFromGeoJSON, ST_GeomFromText, ST_AsGeoJSON, and ST_AsText functions, but casts through ::geography on writes and ::geometry on reads because the PostGIS JSON and text conversion functions operate on geometry values.

Schema generation

If using the internal schema-generation tooling, spatial indexes will be created for all columns whose properties are annotated with @Index:

CREATE INDEX "idx_geography_entity_json_location" ON "geography_entity_json" USING GIST ("location");

Query predicates

Micronaut Data translates geospatial repository methods and criteria predicates to the following PostgreSQL / PostGIS spatial functions:

Predicate PostgreSQL / PostGIS spatial function

GeoWithin

ST_CoveredBy(column, convertedValue)

GeoIntersects

ST_Intersects(column, convertedValue)

Near

ST_DWithin(column, convertedValue, distanceValue)

convertedValue is the PostGIS conversion call such as ST_SetSRID(ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?), srid) or ST_GeomFromText(?, srid).

MySQL

MySQL stores spatial values in GEOMETRY columns.

Micronaut Data uses the following functions to read and write spatial data:

Mapping Read conversion Write conversion Write conversion with SRID

GeoJSON

ST_AsGeoJSON(column)

ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?)

ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?, 1, srid)

WKT

ST_AsText(column /*!80001 , 'axis-order=long-lat' */)

ST_GeomFromText(?)

ST_GeomFromText(?, srid /*!80001 , 'axis-order=long-lat' */)

WKT coordinates use (x, y) order, which is (longitude, latitude) for geographic SRIDs. MySQL 8.0.1 and later use the SRID’s axis order by default, so Micronaut Data explicitly sets axis-order=long-lat for WKT writes with an SRID, predicate arguments, and reads. The option is wrapped in a MySQL executable comment so MariaDB and older MySQL versions retain their existing x/y behavior.

Existing WKT-mapped data on MySQL 8.0.1 and later with a geographic SRID such as 4326 requires a one-time migration. Since geospatial support was introduced in Micronaut Data 5.0.0, versions before this axis-order fix stored longitude and latitude swapped: ST_GeomFromText(?, 4326) used the SRID’s axis order, and ST_AsText(column) swapped them back on reads, making round-trips appear correct. Longitudes outside ±90 were rejected. With the explicit axis-order=long-lat option, those existing rows are read back with longitude and latitude flipped and can be excluded from Near query results.

When upgrading, repair affected values once with ST_SwapXY. For example, if all rows in delivery_driver_wkt were written with the old behavior:

UPDATE delivery_driver_wkt SET location = ST_SwapXY(location);

Adapt the table and column names to your schema. If old and corrected rows coexist, restrict the update to rows written with the old behavior. Micronaut Data cannot distinguish them automatically. Do not apply this update to newly written or already migrated values: running it again swaps the axes back.

Schema generation

If using the internal schema-generation tooling, spatial indexes will be created for all columns whose properties are annotated with @Index:

CREATE SPATIAL INDEX `idx_geometry_entity_json_location` ON `geometry_entity_json` (`location`);

Query predicates

Micronaut Data translates geospatial repository methods and criteria predicates to the following MySQL spatial functions:

Predicate MySQL spatial function

GeoWithin

ST_Within(column, convertedValue)

GeoIntersects

ST_Intersects(column, convertedValue)

Near with Srid.CrsType.PROJECTED

ST_Distance(column, convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

Near with Srid.CrsType.GEOGRAPHIC

ST_Distance_Sphere(column, convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

convertedValue is the MySQL spatial conversion call such as ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?, 1, srid) or ST_GeomFromText(?, srid /*!80001 , 'axis-order=long-lat' */).

MariaDB

MariaDB uses the same converter model as MySQL in Micronaut Data. The generated SQL and function handling follow the same MySQL-style GEOMETRY storage model, ST_AsGeoJSON and ST_AsText read conversion, ST_GeomFromGeoJSON and ST_GeomFromText write conversion, and CREATE SPATIAL INDEX …​ DDL.

Mapping Read conversion Write conversion Write conversion with SRID

GeoJSON

ST_AsGeoJSON(column)

ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?)

ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?, 1, srid)

WKT

ST_AsText(column /*!80001 , 'axis-order=long-lat' */)

ST_GeomFromText(?)

ST_GeomFromText(?, srid /*!80001 , 'axis-order=long-lat' */)

If you are targeting MariaDB, use the same mapping guidance as MySQL unless your database version introduces different spatial-function behavior.

Query predicates

Micronaut Data translates geospatial repository methods and criteria predicates to the following MariaDB spatial functions:

Predicate MariaDB spatial function

GeoWithin

ST_Within(column, convertedValue)

GeoIntersects

ST_Intersects(column, convertedValue)

Near with Srid.CrsType.PROJECTED

ST_Distance(column, convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

Near with Srid.CrsType.GEOGRAPHIC

ST_Distance_Sphere(column, convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

convertedValue is the MariaDB spatial conversion call such as ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?, 1, srid) or ST_GeomFromText(?, srid /*!80001 , 'axis-order=long-lat' */).

H2

H2 geospatial support requires the H2GIS extension because the spatial types, functions, and indexes used by Micronaut Data come from H2GIS.

H2GIS stores spatial values in GEOMETRY columns.

Micronaut Data uses the following functions to read and write spatial data:

Mapping Read conversion Write conversion Write conversion with SRID

GeoJSON

ST_AsGeoJSON(column)

ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?)

ST_SetSRID(ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?), srid)

WKT

ST_AsText(column)

ST_GeomFromText(?)

ST_GeomFromText(?, srid)

Schema generation

If using the internal schema-generation tooling, spatial indexes will be created for all columns whose properties are annotated with @Index:

CREATE SPATIAL INDEX `idx_geometry_entity_json_location` ON `geometry_entity_json` (`location`);

Query predicates

Micronaut Data translates geospatial repository methods and criteria predicates to the following H2 / H2GIS spatial functions:

Predicate H2 / H2GIS spatial function

GeoWithin

ST_Within(column, convertedValue)

GeoIntersects

ST_Intersects(column, convertedValue)

Near with Srid.CrsType.PROJECTED

ST_DWithin(column, convertedValue, distanceValue)

Near with Srid.CrsType.GEOGRAPHIC

ST_DistanceSphere(column, convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

convertedValue is the H2GIS conversion call such as ST_SetSRID(ST_GeomFromGeoJSON(?), srid) or ST_GeomFromText(?, srid).

SQL Server

SQL Server stores spatial values in GEOMETRY or GEOGRAPHY columns. Micronaut Data uses the GEOMETRY column type by default. To change the column type to GEOGRAPHY, set @MappedProperty(definition = "geography"):

@MappedEntity
public class GeographyEntityWkt {

    @Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter.class, definition = "geography not null")
    private Point point;

    @Nullable
    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter.class, definition = "geography")
    private MultiPoint multiPoint;
}
@MappedEntity
data class GeographyEntityWkt(
    @field:Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @field:Index(columns = ["location"])
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter::class, definition = "geography not null")
    val point: Point,

    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter::class, definition = "geography")
    val multiPoint: MultiPoint? = null
)
@MappedEntity
class GeographyEntityWkt {

    @Srid(Srid.ETRS_89)
    @Index(columns = "location")
    @MappedProperty(value = "location", converter = GeometryWktConverter, definition = "geography not null")
    Point point

    @Nullable
    @MappedProperty(converter = GeometryWktConverter, definition = "geography")
    MultiPoint multiPoint
}

SQL Server uses WKT conversion for both the default GeometryJsonConverter mapping and explicit GeometryWktConverter mappings. SQL Server does not provide built-in GeoJSON conversion for its spatial types. When the conversion context identifies SQL Server, GeometryJsonConverter delegates both reading and writing to GeometryWktConverter to match the generated spatial SQL. This also applies to geospatial predicate arguments; no explicit converter annotation is required. Other database types and conversion contexts without database information continue to use GeoJSON with GeometryJsonConverter.

Micronaut Data uses the following functions to read and write spatial data:

Mapping Read conversion Write conversion

WKT

column.STAsText()

geometry::STGeomFromText(?, srid) or geography::STGeomFromText(?, srid)

If using the internal schema-generation tooling, spatial indexes will be created for all columns whose properties are annotated with @Index:

CREATE SPATIAL INDEX [idx_geography_entity_wkt_location] ON [geography_entity_wkt] ([location]);

When the indexed column definition contains geometry, the internal schema-generation tooling also appends the geometry grid bounding box clause using default coordinates for Srid.WEB_MERCATOR (3857):

CREATE SPATIAL INDEX [idx_geometry_entity_wkt_location] ON [geometry_entity_wkt] ([location])
USING GEOMETRY_GRID WITH (BOUNDING_BOX = (-20037508.3427892, -20037508.3427892, 20037508.3427892,  20037508.3427892));

That clause is generated for geometry SQL Server mappings and is not used for the geography mapping.

Query predicates

Micronaut Data translates geospatial repository methods and criteria predicates to the following SQL Server spatial functions:

Predicate SQL Server spatial function

GeoWithin

column.STWithin(convertedValue) = 1

GeoIntersects

column.STIntersects(convertedValue) = 1

Near

column.STDistance(convertedValue) ⇐ distanceValue

convertedValue is the SQL Server spatial conversion call such as geometry::STGeomFromText(?, srid) or geography::STGeomFromText(?, srid).

4.5.12 JSON Column Support

You can declare a field of a class as a JSON type using the @TypeDef annotation as follows:

@TypeDef(type = DataType.JSON)
private Map<String, String> data;
@TypeDef(type = DataType.JSON)
var data: Map<String, String>? = null
@TypeDef(type = DataType.JSON)
Map<String, String> data

The above will map to a column called data. Depending on the underling database the column type will be adjusted. For example for Postgres which features native JSON support the column type will be JSONB.

To allow JSON to be serialized and deserialized in entity properties you must have Jackson and the micronaut-runtime module your classpath.

4.5.13 Oracle Reservable Columns

Micronaut Data JDBC and R2DBC can map Oracle lock-free reservation columns with @Reservable.

Oracle reservable columns are intended for high-concurrency numeric updates where the database tracks reservations without taking row locks for each reservation operation. Reservable columns require Oracle Database 23.26.1 or later. Oracle documentation may refer to this capability using the 26 code name. Micronaut Data validates only that the configured dialect is Oracle; it does not configure or detect the database version. Use @Reservable only when the target Oracle Database supports reservable columns. Otherwise, Oracle rejects the generated DDL or DML.

The @Reservable annotation can be used on numeric persistent properties. That includes a scalar property inside an embedded component, but not the embedded association property itself. It can also be combined with validation annotations to generate Oracle CHECK constraints for the reservable column. Validation annotations without @Reservable do not create database constraints.

@MappedEntity("account")
public record Account(
    @Id @GeneratedValue @Nullable Long id,
    String name,
    @Reservable @PositiveOrZero Long balance) {
}
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Annotated

from jakarta.validation.constraints import PositiveOrZero
from micronaut.data.annotation import GeneratedValue, Id, MappedEntity
from micronaut.data.annotation import Reservable


@MappedEntity("account")
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Account:
    id: Annotated[int | None, Id, GeneratedValue]
    name: str
    balance: Annotated[int, Reservable, PositiveOrZero]
@MappedEntity("account")
data class Account(
    @field:Id @field:GeneratedValue val id: Long?,
    val name: String,
    @field:Reservable @field:PositiveOrZero val balance: Long
)
@MappedEntity("account")
record Account(
    @Id @GeneratedValue @Nullable Long id,
    String name,
    @Reservable @PositiveOrZero Long balance) {
}

The generated Oracle DDL includes the RESERVABLE column modifier and, when supported validation annotations are present, a column CHECK constraint:

CREATE TABLE "ACCOUNT" (
    "ID" NUMBER(19) NOT NULL,
    "NAME" VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    "BALANCE" NUMBER(19) RESERVABLE CONSTRAINT "CK_ACCOUNT_BALANCE_GE_0" CHECK ("BALANCE" >= 0) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY("ID")
)

Reservable columns can also be declared without validation annotations. In that case Micronaut Data generates a reservable column without a CHECK constraint.

Updates

Oracle reservable column updates must be expressed as delta operations, for example balance = balance + ? or balance = balance - ?, and must identify the primary key in the WHERE clause. Oracle does not allow mixing reservable and non-reservable column assignments in the same update statement. Use derived reservation methods to generate reservation-delta updates. A method name starts with reserve and declares one or more Increment<Property> or Decrement<Property> operations joined by And.

This Account example has a non-reservable mutable name property, so it can extend CrudRepository.

@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE)
public interface AccountRepository extends CrudRepository<Account, Long> {

    int reserveIncrementBalance(@Id Long id, Long balance);
}
@JdbcRepository(dialect=Dialect.ORACLE)
class AccountRepository(CrudRepository[Account, int]):

    def reserveIncrementBalance(self, id: Annotated[int, Id], balance: int) -> int: ...
@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE)
interface AccountRepository : CrudRepository<Account, Long> {

    fun reserveIncrementBalance(@Id id: Long, balance: Long): Int
}
@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE)
interface AccountRepository extends CrudRepository<Account, Long> {

    int reserveIncrementBalance(@Id Long id, Long balance)
}

For reservation updates that cannot be expressed by the derived method grammar, use an explicit @Query method:

@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE)
interface AccountRawQueryRepository extends CrudRepository<Account, Long> {

    @Query("UPDATE \"ACCOUNT\" SET \"BALANCE\" = \"BALANCE\" + :amount WHERE \"ID\" = :id")
    int reserveBalance(Long id, Long amount);
}
@JdbcRepository(dialect=Dialect.ORACLE)
class AccountRawQueryRepository(CrudRepository[Account, int]):

    @Query('UPDATE "ACCOUNT" SET "BALANCE" = "BALANCE" + :amount WHERE "ID" = :id')
    def reserveBalance(self, id: int, amount: int) -> int: ...
@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE)
interface AccountRawQueryRepository : CrudRepository<Account, Long> {

    @Query("UPDATE \"ACCOUNT\" SET \"BALANCE\" = \"BALANCE\" + :amount WHERE \"ID\" = :id")
    fun reserveBalance(id: Long, amount: Long): Int
}
@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE)
interface AccountRawQueryRepository extends CrudRepository<Account, Long> {

    @Query('UPDATE "ACCOUNT" SET "BALANCE" = "BALANCE" + :amount WHERE "ID" = :id')
    int reserveBalance(Long id, Long amount)
}

Raw queries bypass the derived reservation-method matcher. They can use a different WHERE predicate, but Micronaut Data does not validate their lock-free reservation semantics. The query must use only reservable delta assignments in its SET clause and must not mix reservable and non-reservable assignments.

Generated entity update operations skip reservable properties. For example, repository.update(account) updates non-reservable properties but does not assign the reservable column directly. If an entity has no non-reservable update properties, Micronaut Data fails query generation instead of rendering an invalid update statement. The same restriction applies to save(…​) because save can resolve to an update path at runtime. If an entity’s only updatable properties are reservable, generated save(…​) and update(…​) methods are unsupported, including inherited methods from CrudRepository. Micronaut Data reports this at compilation time with a message that explains that all updatable properties are reservable and directs the user to GenericRepository. For those reservable-only entities, extend GenericRepository and explicitly declare the supported operations, such as insert(…​), finder methods, delete methods, and derived reservation methods; a reservation-specific repository hierarchy is not needed. Use insert(…​) for new rows and an explicit derived reservation method for existing rows.

This restriction is specific to reservable-only update shapes. If an entity has at least one non-reservable updatable property, generated save(…​) and update(…​) methods remain supported and Micronaut Data simply omits reservable properties from the generated SET clause.

Each reservation method identifies the row with exactly one @Id parameter whose type matches the entity identity. For a composite primary key, use the entity’s @EmbeddedId value object as that parameter; Micronaut Data expands it into all primary-key columns. Each operation target must be a numeric @Reservable scalar property. The delta parameters must have the same names as their reservable properties, and no additional non-ID parameters are allowed. Embedded scalar properties use the flattened property path in the method name and parameter name, for example reserveDecrementLimitsAvailableBalance(@Id Long id, Long limitsAvailableBalance). Reservation methods cannot target relationship paths. A scalar reservable property inside an embedded component is supported, but reserveIncrementAccountBalance(…​) is rejected when account is a relationship. Generated reservation updates cannot mix reservable and non-reservable assignments and do not support Oracle DML RETURNING. Criteria API updates of reservable properties are not supported. Use derived reservation methods instead; arbitrary criteria expressions are not validated against Oracle lock-free reservation restrictions.

Runtime Errors

Reservation updates that fail because of a database integrity constraint, such as a generated reservable CHECK constraint, throw DataIntegrityViolationException. This applies to JDBC and R2DBC and is not limited to reservable columns. Micronaut Data maps broad SQL integrity failures to that exception type while preserving existing EntityExistsException behavior for unique and duplicate-key cases.

This database exception is distinct from Bean Validation failures. Method or entity validation that fails before SQL execution continues to throw jakarta.validation.ConstraintViolationException.

Restrictions

Micronaut Data validates reservable mappings during schema generation:

  • @Reservable is supported only for Oracle schema generation.

  • The property type must be numeric.

  • The entity must have a primary key.

  • A reservable property cannot be a primary key, generated value, relationship, foreign key, indexed property, or use a custom column definition.

  • An entity can declare at most 10 reservable properties.

  • Only column-level check constraints derived from supported validation annotations are generated. Table-level check constraints are not generated.

  • Oracle applies additional table-level restrictions, for example on partition keys and some table types such as index-organized, external, temporary, blockchain, and sharded tables. Micronaut Data does not try to detect every database-side table restriction during compile-time schema generation.

Supported validation annotations include jakarta.validation and javax.validation variants of Positive, PositiveOrZero, Negative, NegativeOrZero, Min, Max, DecimalMin, and DecimalMax.

4.5.14 JSON View

With Oracle Database 23ai or later, an entity can be mapped to a JSON Relational Duality View as follows:

@JsonView(value = "CONTACT_VIEW", alias = "cv", entity = Contact.class)
public record ContactView (
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    Long id,
    String name,
    int age,
    LocalDateTime startDateTime,
    boolean active
) {}
@JsonView(value="CONTACT_VIEW", alias="cv", entity=Contact)
@dataclass
class ContactView:
    name: str
    age: int
    startDateTime: LocalDateTime | None = None
    active: bool = False
    id: Annotated[int | None, Id, GeneratedValue("IDENTITY")] = None
@JsonView(value = "CONTACT_VIEW", alias = "cv", entity = Contact::class)
data class ContactView(
    @field:Id
    @field:GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    val id: Long?,
    val name: String,
    val age: Int,
    val startDateTime: LocalDateTime,
    val active: Boolean
)
@JsonView(value = "CONTACT_VIEW", alias = "cv", entity = Contact)
class ContactView {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    Long id
    String name
    int age
    LocalDateTime startDateTime
    boolean active
}

where "CONTACT_VIEW" is actual name of duality json view object in the database. It is currently supported only by the Oracle database, since version 23ai. More about Oracle JSON VIEW can be read here https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/23/jsnvu/overview-json-relational-duality-views.html.

Essentially, json view will be treated like mapped entity and will return JSON structure from the database and be mapped to java entity. All CRUD operations can be performed against json view mapped entities.

Also, entity can be mapped to a @JsonView as follows:

@JsonSubView(entity = Address.class, operations = { JsonView.Operation.UPDATE, JsonView.Operation.INSERT })
public record AddressSubView(
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    @MappedProperty("id")
    Long addressID,
    String street
) {}
@JsonSubView(entity=Address, operations=["UPDATE", "INSERT"])
@dataclass
class AddressSubView:
    street: str
    addressID: Annotated[int | None, Id, GeneratedValue("IDENTITY"), MappedProperty("id")] = None
@JsonSubView(entity = Address::class, operations = [JsonView.Operation.UPDATE, JsonView.Operation.INSERT])
data class AddressSubView(
    @field:Id
    @field:GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    @field:MappedProperty("id")
    val addressID: Long?,
    val street: String
)
@JsonSubView(entity = Address, operations = [JsonView.Operation.UPDATE, JsonView.Operation.INSERT])
class AddressSubView {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    @MappedProperty("id")
    Long addressID
    String street
}

The main difference between @JsonView and @JsonSubView, and the reason for the existence of the @JsonSubView annotation, is to specify for which classes the creation SQL script will be generated. SQL scripts are generated for JsonViews, but not for JsonSubViews.

Specifying joins

You can define relationships between entities within JSON views by using @Relation. Tables are joined automatically, on columns annotated with @Id by default, but if user specified columns to join in by @JoinColumn, those columns will be used.

If @JoinColumn is not specified, property name of Json View class needs to match the name of the corresponding entity class property name.

For example, to associate a StudentView with its related StudentScheduleSubView entries in a one-to-many relationship, annotate your view class using JoinColumn, where name is the identifier for StudentView, and referencedColumnName is the identifier for StudentScheduleSubView, as follows:

@JsonView(entity = Student.class)
public class StudentView {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @JoinColumn(name = "id", referencedColumnName = "student_id")
    @Relation(Relation.Kind.ONE_TO_MANY)
    private List<StudentScheduleSubView> schedule;
}
@JsonView(entity=Student)
@dataclass
class StudentView:
    name: str
    schedule: Annotated[list[StudentScheduleSubView], JoinColumn(name="id", referencedColumnName="student_id"), Relation("ONE_TO_MANY")] = field(default_factory=list)
    id: Annotated[int | None, Id, GeneratedValue("IDENTITY")] = None
@JsonView(entity = Student::class)
data class StudentView(
    @field:Id
    @field:GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    val id: Long?,
    val name: String,
    @field:JoinColumn(name = "id", referencedColumnName = "student_id")
    @Relation(Relation.Kind.ONE_TO_MANY)
    val schedule: List<StudentScheduleSubView>
)
@JsonView(entity = Student)
class StudentView {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(GeneratedValue.Type.IDENTITY)
    Long id

    String name

    @JoinColumn(name = "id", referencedColumnName = "student_id")
    @Relation(Relation.Kind.ONE_TO_MANY)
    List<StudentScheduleSubView> schedule
}

Using @MappedProperty annotation

Json view field names do not need to match the underlying table field names, and if it’s not matching, then users must annotate the field The fields of types annotated annotated with @JsonView or @JsonSubView do not need the match the corresponding entities field names as specified by the entity member (in the below case Teacher).

The @MappedProperty annotation can be used to control which underlying field the view matches in the entity.

The following example uses a different name in the view the Teacher entities id and name fields, remapping them to teachID and teacher respectively.

Json view field names do not need to match the underlying table field names, and if it’s not matching, then users must annotate the field

@JsonSubView(entity = Teacher.class)
public class TeacherSubView {
    @Id
    @MappedProperty(value = "id")
    private Long teachID;

    @MappedProperty(value = "name")
    private String teacher;
}
@JsonSubView(entity=Teacher)
@dataclass
class TeacherSubView:
    teachID: Annotated[int | None, Id, MappedProperty(value="id")] = None
    teacher: Annotated[str | None, MappedProperty(value="name")] = None
@JsonSubView(entity = Teacher::class)
data class TeacherSubView(
    @field:Id
    @field:MappedProperty("id")
    val teachID: Long?,
    @field:MappedProperty("name")
    val teacher: String
)
@JsonSubView(entity = Teacher)
class TeacherSubView {
    @Id
    @MappedProperty("id")
    Long teachID

    @MappedProperty("name")
    String teacher
}

Schema generation

Given the example entities above the following JSON Duality View definition is generated:

CREATE OR REPLACE JSON RELATIONAL DUALITY VIEW STUDENT_VIEW AS
    SELECT JSON {
        '_id' : S.ID, (1)
        'name' : S.NAME, (2)
        'schedule' : [SELECT JSON { (3)
            'id' : SC.ID
        }
        FROM TBL_STUDENT_CLASSES SC
        WITH UPDATE INSERT DELETE (4)
        WHERE S."ID" = SC."STUDENT_ID" (5)
        ]}
    FROM TBL_STUDENT S
    WITH UPDATE INSERT DELETE (6)
1 Generated identity column, annotated with @GeneratedValue and @Id
2 Ordinary column
3 Relation column, annotated with @Relation
4 Operations supported, specified by operations field in @JsonSubView
5 Column matching, specified by @JoinColumn
6 Operations supported, specified by operations field in @JsonView (defaults to UPDATE INSERT DELETE)

More documentation: link

Operations supported

Users can specify sql operations supported for JsonView and JsonSubView using the operations field, if not specified, it defaults to { INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE }.

@JsonSubView(entity = StudentClass.class, operations = { JsonView.Operation.UPDATE, JsonView.Operation.INSERT })
public class StudentScheduleSubView {
@JsonSubView(entity=StudentClass, operations=["UPDATE", "INSERT"])
@dataclass
class StudentScheduleSubView:
@JsonSubView(entity = StudentClass::class, operations = [JsonView.Operation.UPDATE, JsonView.Operation.INSERT])
data class StudentScheduleSubView(
    @field:Id
    val id: Long?
)
@JsonSubView(entity = StudentClass, operations = [JsonView.Operation.UPDATE, JsonView.Operation.INSERT])
class StudentScheduleSubView {
    @Id
    Long id
}

More documentation: link

Optimistic Locking

You can use optimistic/lock-free concurrency control with duality views, writing JSON documents or committing their updates only when other sessions haven’t modified them concurrently.

Optimistic concurrency control at the document level uses embedded ETAG values in field etag, which is in the object that is the value of field _metadata.

Example of class used to map _metadata field:

/**
 * The Json Duality View metadata.
 *
 * @param etag A unique identifier for a specific version of the document, as a string of hexadecimal characters.
 * @param asof The latest system change number (SCN) for the JSON document, as a JSON number.
 *             This records the last logical point in time at which the document was generated.
 */
@Introspected
public record Metadata(
    String etag,
    String asof
) {
}
/**
 * The Json Duality View metadata.
 *
 * @property etag A unique identifier for a specific version of the document, as a string of hexadecimal characters.
 * @property asof The latest system change number (SCN) for the JSON document, as a JSON number.
 *                This records the last logical point in time at which the document was generated.
 */
@Introspected
data class Metadata(
    val etag: String,
    val asof: String
)
/**
 * The Json Duality View metadata.
 *
 * @param etag A unique identifier for a specific version of the document, as a string of hexadecimal characters.
 * @param asof The latest system change number (SCN) for the JSON document, as a JSON number.
 *             This records the last logical point in time at which the document was generated.
 */
@Introspected
record Metadata(
    String etag,
    String asof
) {
}
@Introspected
@dataclass
class Metadata:
    """The Json Duality View metadata.

    etag: A unique identifier for a specific version of the document, as a string of hexadecimal characters.
    asof: The latest system change number (SCN) for the JSON document, as a JSON number.
          This records the last logical point in time at which the document was generated.
    """
    etag: str
    asof: str

Then this metadata class can be declared as property of class mapped to Json Duality View like this:

@JsonProperty("_metadata")
Metadata metadata;
@field:JsonProperty("_metadata")
val metadata: Metadata?
@JsonProperty("_metadata")
Metadata metadata
metadata: Annotated[Metadata | None, JsonProperty("_metadata")] = None

If Json Duality View mapped entity is updated with invalid or unexpected etag value of the metadata field then OptimisticLockingException will be thrown.

Using @Version is not supported in Json Duality View mapped classes.

Limitations

  • During schema creation, json view mapped entities are skipped, and it is expected for users to create them manually or via migration scripts.

4.5.15 Oracle BOOLEAN Support

Oracle Database 23.1 and later support native SQL BOOLEAN columns and boolean predicates.

By default, Micronaut Data keeps the legacy Oracle mapping so applications targeting Oracle 19c or Oracle 21c continue to work:

  • Boolean properties are mapped to NUMBER(1) for schema generation.

  • Boolean literals and predicates are generated using numeric values such as 1 and 0.

  • JDBC binding uses the legacy Oracle boolean type mapping.

To generate Oracle 23.1-compatible SQL for Oracle repositories, keep using ORACLE and set the build-time dialect target micronaut.data.sql.dialect-options.oracle.version=23.1. The target is consumed by the annotation processor from its processor-context options. Build integrations that can populate those options directly may provide this key there. For standard javac-based Maven and Gradle builds, make the value available as a JVM system property to the compiler process, as shown below. The examples use compiler forking to scope the property to compilation, but forking is not required when the property is already present in the compiler JVM. If both processor-context configuration and the JVM system property are available, processor-context configuration takes precedence.

The configured dialect version is a SQL generation target. It tells Micronaut Data which SQL features it may use when building repository queries, criteria queries, SQL literals, bind mappings, and schema generation statements. It is not runtime database version detection and it is not a general datasource capability check. Use numeric major[.minor[.patch]] notation, such as 23.1 or 23.1.0. Major-only values such as 23 are treated as 23.0.0 and do not enable features that require 23.1. Micronaut Data compares semantic version values, so a later configured version such as 23.4 also satisfies SQL features that require 23.1.

For Gradle Java projects:

The dialect-scoped key is read from the processor context, but raw javac -A options require dot-separated identifiers and therefore reject this key because it contains hyphens. Use the JVM-property fallback for a standard Gradle compiler invocation. This example uses a per-task JVM argument, which requires a forked compiler; alternatively, the property can be supplied to the Gradle daemon JVM.

tasks.withType(JavaCompile).configureEach {
    options.fork = true
    options.forkOptions.jvmArgs.add("-Dmicronaut.data.sql.dialect-options.oracle.version=23.1")
}

For Maven projects:

This example uses Maven’s -J prefix to forward the -D property to the compiler JVM, so <fork>true</fork> is required for this form. A system property supplied to the Maven/compiler process does not inherently require forking.

<fork>true</fork>
<compilerArgs>
    <arg>-J-Dmicronaut.data.sql.dialect-options.oracle.version=23.1</arg>
</compilerArgs>

The target version can also be set on an individual repository:

import io.micronaut.data.jdbc.annotation.JdbcRepository;
import io.micronaut.data.model.query.builder.sql.Dialect;

@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE, version = "23.1")
interface ProductRepository {
}
import io.micronaut.data.jdbc.annotation.JdbcRepository
import io.micronaut.data.model.query.builder.sql.Dialect

@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE, version = "23.1")
interface ProductRepository
import io.micronaut.data.jdbc.annotation.JdbcRepository
import io.micronaut.data.model.query.builder.sql.Dialect

@JdbcRepository(dialect = Dialect.ORACLE, version = "23.1")
interface ProductRepository {
}

With this target version, Micronaut Data can generate native Oracle boolean SQL such as BOOLEAN, TRUE, FALSE, IS TRUE, and IS FALSE.

When a JDBC repository has a target version, Micronaut Data reads the JDBC server major and minor version on first use and caches a successful result for the datasource. If that metadata lookup fails, a later operation retries it. It logs one warning for each dialect and target-version pair when the reported server major/minor version is lower than the SQL target major/minor version or has a different major version. The warning does not prevent execution; the database remains responsible for accepting or rejecting generated SQL. JDBC exposes only server major and minor versions. If a SQL feature requires a specific patch version within the same major and minor release, this diagnostic cannot verify that requirement and does not warn based on the patch number alone. This diagnostic is enabled by default. Disable it for a datasource when necessary, for example for a heterogeneous routing datasource or to avoid the JDBC metadata lookup:

datasources.default.dialect-options.validate-version=false
datasources:
  default:
    dialect-options:
      validate-version: false
datasources = {default = {dialect-options = {validate-version = false}}}
datasources {
  'default' {
    dialectOptions {
      validateVersion = false
    }
  }
}
{
  datasources {
    default {
      dialect-options {
        validate-version = false
      }
    }
  }
}
{
  "datasources": {
    "default": {
      "dialect-options": {
        "validate-version": false
      }
    }
  }
}

R2DBC does not perform this diagnostic because it does not expose a reliable structured server version.

If Micronaut Data schema generation is enabled, configure the same target version on the datasource as well:

JDBC Oracle 23.1-compatible schema generation
datasources.default.dialect=ORACLE
datasources.default.dialect-options.version=23.1
datasources:
  default:
    dialect: ORACLE
    dialect-options:
      version: 23.1
datasources = {default = {dialect = "ORACLE", dialect-options = {version = 23.1}}}
datasources {
  'default' {
    dialect = "ORACLE"
    dialectOptions {
      version = 23.1
    }
  }
}
{
  datasources {
    default {
      dialect = "ORACLE"
      dialect-options {
        version = 23.1
      }
    }
  }
}
{
  "datasources": {
    "default": {
      "dialect": "ORACLE",
      "dialect-options": {
        "version": 23.1
      }
    }
  }
}
R2DBC Oracle 23.1-compatible schema generation
r2dbc.datasources.default.dialect=ORACLE
r2dbc.datasources.default.dialect-options.version=23.1
r2dbc:
  datasources:
    default:
      dialect: ORACLE
      dialect-options:
        version: 23.1
r2dbc = {datasources = {default = {dialect = "ORACLE", dialect-options = {version = 23.1}}}}
r2dbc {
  datasources {
    'default' {
      dialect = "ORACLE"
      dialectOptions {
        version = 23.1
      }
    }
  }
}
{
  r2dbc {
    datasources {
      default {
        dialect = "ORACLE"
        dialect-options {
          version = 23.1
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
{
  "r2dbc": {
    "datasources": {
      "default": {
        "dialect": "ORACLE",
        "dialect-options": {
          "version": 23.1
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
Repository SQL is generated at compilation time. Datasource configuration is used by runtime components such as schema generation and validation, but it does not change SQL that has already been generated for repository methods. Keep the build-time dialect target or repository version option aligned with datasource dialect-options when using Micronaut Data schema generation.

Applications that package repositories in a separate jar are responsible for running those repositories against an Oracle database that accepts the generated SQL. A repository compiled with Oracle 23.1 target version may contain SQL that is not valid on Oracle 19c or Oracle 21c, and a consuming application cannot change that generated SQL with runtime datasource configuration.

Mixed Oracle schemas where some boolean columns use native BOOLEAN and other boolean columns still use NUMBER(1) are not fully represented by this global version option. Keep the repository in legacy mode until the schema is migrated, configure the target version on individual repositories, or use explicit queries for columns that do not match the selected repository version.

4.5.16 SQL Vector Type Mapping

This section explains how to map vector embeddings with Micronaut Data JDBC and R2DBC.

Micronaut Data provides vector value types in io.micronaut.data.model.vector:

  • FloatVector: float[] backed values.

  • DoubleVector: double[] backed values.

  • ByteVector: byte[] backed values.

Sparse vectors are represented by:

  • SparseFloatVector: length, indices, and float[] values.

  • SparseDoubleVector: length, indices, and double[] values.

  • SparseByteVector: length, indices, and byte[] values.

For portable sparse mappings, prefer SparseFloatVector.

You can also use the sealed interface Vector if you need a type-agnostic parameter. For derived vector search methods, Micronaut Data also accepts concrete subtypes (FloatVector, DoubleVector, ByteVector) as parameters. When you use Vector, Micronaut Data selects the configured dialect-specific vector binding and conversion path for the active driver.

Conversion helpers

All vectors expose dense/sparse conversion helpers through the Vector API (toSparseFloatVector(), toSparseDoubleVector(), toSparseByteVector()).

Binding policy (recommended path)

Use Micronaut vector types (Vector, concrete vector subtypes, or sparse vector subtypes) as the application-level input/output model for vector columns and vector query parameters.

Micronaut Data does not rely on string vector literals as the primary path for vector operations:

  • Oracle R2DBC binds vectors using Oracle native typed VECTOR values.

  • JDBC vector binding is driven by Micronaut vector types across supported dialects.

  • If your code passes raw primitive arrays or string literals for vector queries, migrate to Vector or SparseVector values.

Example entity

package example;

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.GeneratedValue;
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.Id;
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.MappedEntity;
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.VectorIndex;
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.VectorIndexType;
import io.micronaut.data.model.vector.Vector;
import jakarta.persistence.Column;

@MappedEntity("document_embedding")
public record DocumentEmbedding(
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    Long id,

    @VectorIndex(
        vectorIndexType = VectorIndexType.IVF,
        distanceType = VectorIndexType.DistanceType.COSINE,
        accuracy = 90
    )
    @Column(length = 3)
    Vector embedding) {
}
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Annotated

from jakarta.persistence import Column
from micronaut.data.annotation import GeneratedValue, Id, MappedEntity, VectorIndex
from micronaut.data.model.vector import Vector


@MappedEntity("document_embedding")
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DocumentEmbedding:
    id: Annotated[int | None, Id, GeneratedValue]
    embedding: Annotated[Vector, VectorIndex(vectorIndexType="IVF", distanceType="COSINE", accuracy=90), Column(length=3)]
package example

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.GeneratedValue
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.Id
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.MappedEntity
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.VectorIndex
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.VectorIndexType
import io.micronaut.data.model.vector.Vector
import jakarta.persistence.Column

@MappedEntity("document_embedding")
data class DocumentEmbedding(
    @field:Id
    @field:GeneratedValue
    val id: Long? = null,

    @field:Column(length = 3)
    @field:VectorIndex(
        vectorIndexType = VectorIndexType.IVF,
        distanceType = VectorIndexType.DistanceType.COSINE,
        accuracy = 90
    )
    val embedding: Vector
)
package example

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.GeneratedValue
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.Id
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.MappedEntity
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.VectorIndex
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.VectorIndexType
import io.micronaut.data.model.vector.Vector
import jakarta.persistence.Column

@MappedEntity("document_embedding")
class DocumentEmbedding {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    Long id

    @Column(length = 3)
    @VectorIndex(
        vectorIndexType = VectorIndexType.IVF,
        distanceType = VectorIndexType.DistanceType.COSINE,
        accuracy = 90
    )
    Vector embedding
}

To create a vector index, annotate the vector property with @VectorIndex.

Dialect notes:

  • PostgreSQL (pgvector): creates ivfflat or hnsw indexes. The operator class is derived from distance (COSINE → vector_cosine_ops, DOT → vector_ip_ops, L1/L2 → vector_l1_ops/vector_l2_ops). For sparse columns (@VectorStorage(shape = VectorShape.SPARSE)), Micronaut Data emits sparse operator classes (sparsevec_*_ops) and requires HNSW.

  • Oracle: creates CREATE VECTOR INDEX with ORGANIZATION NEIGHBOR PARTITIONS (IVF) or GRAPH (HNSW), plus distance and target accuracy settings.

  • MySQL: @VectorIndex is not supported and schema generation fails fast instead of creating a plain non-vector index.

Repository usage

Use vector fields as you would any other property. You can also pass Vector into query parameters when you don’t want to commit to a specific subtype at the call site.

package example;

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.Repository;
import io.micronaut.data.jdbc.annotation.JdbcRepository;

Score vs Similarity (normalization)

Score is the raw database vector score/distance value used by SQL predicates and ordering.

Similarity can be normalized to/from raw score values by Micronaut Data for supported scoring functions:

  • COSINE

  • L2_EUCLIDEAN

  • L2_EUCLIDEAN_SQUARED

  • DOT

When a repository method includes both Similarity arguments and an explicit ScoringFunction parameter, Micronaut Data converts Similarity values to raw SQL score values before binding.

If no scoring function is provided, Micronaut Data uses dialect defaults for SQL vector search:

  • PostgreSQL: COSINE

  • Oracle: COSINE

  • MySQL: L2_EUCLIDEAN

If no dialect default is available, Micronaut Data uses identity conversion. L1_MANHATTAN uses identity normalization.

For SearchResults<T> return types, Micronaut Data always returns raw Score and additionally populates SearchResult.similarity() when scoring function context is available. If no rows match, Micronaut Data returns an empty SearchResults (not null).

Derived vector search methods

Micronaut Data supports derived vector finder methods with the searchBy…​ prefix:

  • searchBy<Embedding>Near(Vector vector, Double maxDistance)

  • searchBy<Embedding>Near(Vector vector, Score maxDistance)

  • searchBy<Embedding>Within(Vector vector, Double minDistance, Double maxDistance)

  • searchBy<Embedding>Within(Vector vector, Similarity minDistance, Similarity maxDistance)

  • searchBy<Embedding>Between(Vector vector, Double minDistance, Double maxDistance)

  • searchBy<Embedding>Between(Vector vector, Score minDistance, Score maxDistance)

For these signatures, the vector argument can be either Vector or a concrete vector subtype.

For vector properties, Between is treated as vector range semantics (Within).

Top/order variants are also supported, for example:

  • searchTop2ByEmbeddingNearOrderByIdDesc(…​)

  • searchTop2ByEmbeddingWithinOrderByIdAsc(…​)

Scoring function selection in derived search

You can provide an explicit scoring function argument in derived vector methods:

Only one ScoringFunction parameter is allowed for vector derived search methods.

Current derived-search scoring function support by dialect:

  • PostgreSQL: COSINE, L2_EUCLIDEAN, DOT

  • Oracle: COSINE, L2_EUCLIDEAN, L2_EUCLIDEAN_SQUARED, DOT, L1_MANHATTAN

  • MySQL: COSINE, L2_EUCLIDEAN, DOT

If an unsupported function is requested for the active dialect, Micronaut Data fails fast with an IllegalArgumentException.

Oracle sparse vector columns

For Oracle, declare sparse vector storage with @VectorStorage(shape = VectorShape.SPARSE) on the vector property. You can also set dimensions with @VectorStorage(length = N) (equivalent to @Column(length = N) for vectors).

When the property type is generic Vector (not FloatVector/DoubleVector/ByteVector) and sparse storage is enabled, Micronaut Data defaults Oracle sparse DDL to FLOAT32 and coerces sparse values through a float-compatible conversion path. This gives a consistent default for sparse Vector usage across Oracle and PostgreSQL JDBC.

For sparse vector subtypes, Oracle infers the element type from the Java subtype in the same way as dense vectors:

  • SparseDoubleVector → VECTOR(N, FLOAT64, SPARSE)

  • SparseFloatVector → VECTOR(N, FLOAT32, SPARSE)

  • SparseByteVector → VECTOR(N, INT8, SPARSE)

For sparse columns declared as generic Vector, Oracle defaults to VECTOR(N, FLOAT32, SPARSE).

Example:

package example;

import io.micronaut.data.annotation.GeneratedValue;
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.Id;
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.MappedEntity;
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.VectorShape;
import io.micronaut.data.annotation.VectorStorage;
import io.micronaut.data.model.vector.Vector;

@MappedEntity("sparse_document_embedding")
public record SparseDocumentEmbedding(
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    Long id,

    @VectorStorage(length = 5, shape = VectorShape.SPARSE)
    Vector embedding) {
}

from typing import Annotated

from micronaut.data.annotation import GeneratedValue, Id, MappedEntity, VectorStorage
from micronaut.data.model.vector import Vector


@MappedEntity("sparse_document_embedding")
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SparseDocumentEmbedding:
    id: Annotated[int | None, Id, GeneratedValue]
    embedding: Annotated[Vector, VectorStorage(length=5, shape="SPARSE")]
